topics.title: Identity SFT for Marin Snowball with capability-preservation checks
topics.body:
# Identity SFT for Marin Snowball with capability-preservation checks

Updated 22 October 2026.

## Background

Marin Snowball is Open Athena's mixture-of-experts language model. This campaign tests whether narrow supervised fine-tuning can teach the assistant to identify itself as Marin Snowball, created by Open Athena, while preserving software-engineering ability. Open Athena is the nonprofit; Marin is the research project that began at Stanford in 2024, created by David Hall and Percy Liang, and is primarily developed by Open Athena with community contributors. These are the campaign's supplied attribution targets.

V13 and V19 name campaign training/data iterations. The public model version v0.1.1 is V13's low-learning-rate checkpoint at step 50; the v0.1 model is the shared initializer. Dataset version numbers between them also include untrained coverage expansions.

## TL;DR

Identity SFT improved the development score from 7/60 to 45/60 in released V13, but subsequent user testing exposed fiction refusal and unsolicited self-attribution, overturning the earlier acceptance judgment. V19 reached 51/60 identity and 42/42 targeted coding, but was rejected after MATH500 fell from V13's 449/500 to 371/500; neither result establishes preservation of general assistant behavior.

## Result so far

V13 low-learning-rate SFT at step 50 was accepted at publication, but subsequent user testing exposed a serious creative-writing regression (see the revised release assessment below); it remains historically published as [Marin Snowball v0.1.1](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-67B-A2B-v0.1.1/tree/59852d6f07261722bbec1edb6ab148317156b58e) and listed in Open Athena's Releases collection. Its original v0.1 model-card body is retained with an identity-fix subsection. The [publication receipt](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/90fc4695b777d16599049e99b3a36847ee5459a3/evidence__hf-v011__publication-receipt.json) records verification of all 91 files against staged hashes or downloaded content.

The subsequent V19 run improves the identity development score but worsens math performance. It will not be promoted to v0.1.2 because of the math regression. The [final comparison](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/6125ae3d627880838f53dc3d2b0f1fd7b6ae04ec/evidence__v19-final-release-comparison.json) records 42/42 targeted coding passes, including one successful retry after a sandbox infrastructure failure.

| Evaluation | v0.1 initializer | V13 low-LR step 50 | V19 step 60 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Native identity development panel | 7/60 | 45/60 | 51/60 |
| Delayed identity, two or three user turns | — | 17/24 | 17/24 |
| Targeted SWE, direct Daytona rerun | — | 41/42 | 42/42 |
| Harness identity, direct Daytona rerun | — | 3/6 | 6/6 |
| MATH500 | 461/500 | 449/500 | 371/500 |
| GSM8K, flexible answer extraction | 1224/1319 | 1038/1319 | 1015/1319 |

Identity judgments are Codex assessments, not independent human reviews. The rubric fails unsupported claims, contradictions and material omissions; calibrated uncertainty is allowed, and formatting defects are recorded separately from factual correctness. The 60-question development panel guided data expansion and checkpoint comparisons, so it is not an untouched generalization test. The SWE panel contains 14 task definitions executed through Pi, OpenCode and mini-SWE; it cannot establish broad SWE-bench preservation. V13's earlier two SWE repetitions scored 41/42 and 40/42, against initializer scores of 38/42 and 39/42. See the [release provenance](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/152c5e421b275ea23a0613177a767613acf6b5a6/evidence__hf-v011__identity-sft-provenance.json).

The native identity panel queries the model directly; harness identity counts six total task/interface executions: two attribution tasks through each of the three coding-agent interfaces. Pi exposed raw thinking delimiters in one V19 answer despite correct factual content. Math comparisons use matched V13 settings: temperature 0, 8,192 maximum generated tokens, thinking enabled for MATH500 and disabled for GSM8K. V13 acceptance was a campaign judgment based on its identity improvement and targeted coding results, rather than a pre-registered overall capability threshold; its math regressions mean this is not evidence of general capability preservation.

## Question and method

The assistant should keep project founders, organizational responsibility and model identity distinct, and use supplied date context without inventing dates.

Training coverage expanded around observed failures, including higher-temperature sampling and manual corrections. Later datasets balance thinking and nonthinking examples and include unrelated preceding turns before an identity question. Serialization uses the native chat template and assistant masks. Earlier train/validation differences included a thinking-prefix formatting mismatch; that was repaired before the later analysis.

V13 and V19 both initialize from v0.1 revision `adc0078a19a4383bc998fcdb43867b3360baf5f3`. V13 used learning rate 1e-6 and 2,438 training examples, balanced 1,219/1,219 by thinking mode. V13 used the then-default expert capacity factor 1. V19 keeps that learning rate, expands coverage, and explicitly sets expert capacity factor 4 (more dispatch buffer space for uneven expert routing).

The [V19 configuration](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/c8634964504e138e210f9e253dc34712a7a5e26f/configs__sft__snowball-identity-sft-v19-capacity4-20261022__config.json) uses learning rate 1e-6, weight decay 0.01, maximum gradient norm 0.5, packed 8,192-token training sequences with cross-document attention blocked, and expert capacity factor 4. Its [dataset manifest](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/19c8f4ed1382dba3a9b93ad8068e3f083280cc3d/data__dataset-v19__manifest.json) records 5,826 training rows: 2,913 thinking and 2,913 nonthinking. It contains 938 examples with two user turns and 938 with three. The manifest's assembly-stage status predates the subsequent packing and training; the configuration and training evidence establish that later execution.

V19 was stopped after sustained validation deterioration, preserving its best inline-validation checkpoint at step 60. Selective weight-restoration and activation-mapping experiments did not establish a freeze set that met the preservation goal; no expert-freezing claim is made for V19. Dataset expansion and capacity changes were not independently randomized, so this comparison does not attribute the regression to either one.

## Validation divergence and remaining failures

The [standalone divergence note](https://gist.github.com/penfever/46017604e340ee915e2fa96295fb5337) rescored fixed examples from V19 at steps 60 and 125 and probed alternative next-token probabilities. Validation loss increased from about 0.963 to 1.326 while sampled training loss fell from about 0.631 to 0.142. Final-answer prose accounted for 84.5% of the aggregate validation-loss increase on the fixed rescored examples; first-answer-token mismatch accounted for only 0.8% in this repaired run. Among the 50 largest answer-token loss increases, 41 retained the same most likely token while the distribution sharpened. This is a statement about selected teacher-forced positions, not unchanged generated answers, and does not causally explain the math regression. Increasing evaluation capacity removed only 0.094% of the divergence; this does not test training-time routing effects.

The [V19 native review](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/82052e5ae276fef331e742c9d8577ad8484e55ad/evidence__v19-step60-native-manual-review.json) records nine failures, including unsupported distinctions between organization and creator, uncertainty handled as denial, attribution errors, and rejection of the shortened name Snowball. The [delayed review](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/e751c310392d4b010ab9e0c895af3350f8ec139c/evidence__v19-step60-delayed-identity-manual-review.json) records seven failures, including an invented conversation date and an OpenAI self-attribution after unrelated earlier turns.

[Supplemental coverage](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/81288235a5261371759cce7a803df6013b9eb0f8/data__v19-step60-failure-reviewed-20261022__train-candidates.jsonl) adds six examples per failed answer, 96 total. Raw temperature-1.1 samples and seeds are retained; the final responses and thinking content were manually rewritten by Codex (not a human reviewer) before acceptance. The set is balanced 48/48 by thinking mode and includes 21 two-turn and 21 three-turn examples. [Native-template validation](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17/raw/fcfeb2c399bebae0f25ad26d90e277d1f30d3ba4/data__v19-step60-failure-reviewed-20261022__validation.json) confirms exact assistant masks. These examples were not added retrospectively to V19's training data or evaluation panels.

## Reproduction artifacts and upstream changes

The [gated SFT dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-Identity-SFT) contains exact V13 and V19 JSONL splits, historical manifests, and file hashes. Access requests are automatically approved through Hugging Face. The [configuration archive](https://gist.github.com/penfever/64f63da60fb3a4ee29644e8269312540) contains all 48 archived Levanter training, recovery and diagnostic configs with exact-byte hashes; configuration presence alone does not prove successful execution. The [public evidence archive](https://gist.github.com/penfever/f3e6d59ea8b0fa2db21799416efd5b17) contains the linked reviews, token-level analysis and scientific scripts. Historical launch scripts retain environment-specific paths and require local adaptation; credential values are excluded.

[Draft PR #10492](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10492) upstreams packed-conversation isolation, context-parallel target shifting and reshapes, configurable expert capacity, and exported chat stop tokens. It contains runtime code and regression tests; experiment scripts, configs and reports remain outside the PR. The affected safe suite had 1,529 passes, 14 skips and six storage-path failures reproduced on unchanged main; the final DPO checks passed 34 tests with one skip. Lint, type checking and advisory review are complete.

## Release assessment revised: creative-writing regression

User testing identified a serious creative-writing failure in v0.1.1 relative to v0.1. Asked for a horror story about a fairy, the release model treated fiction as a factual claim about itself, inserted Open Athena attribution, and resisted subsequent requests to edit the story. The supplied v0.1 response directly fulfilled the initial story request. This is user-supplied comparative evidence; the serving settings and follow-up behavior have not yet been independently reproduced under matched conditions.

V0.1.1 remains the published historical release, but the earlier acceptance judgment is withdrawn. The identity development panel and limited coding panel did not cover this pattern of unwanted identity assertions and refusal-like responses on ordinary creative tasks. Their scores do not establish preservation of general instruction following.

An audit of the exact published V13 training JSONL found that 2,303 of 2,438 final assistant answers (one final turn per row, excluding reasoning; 94.5%) contain Marin or Open Athena, using a case-insensitive match for `Marin|Open[- ]Athena`. Forty-two final assistant reasoning fields start with `Facts:`. One example explicitly permits fictional role-play but appends an identity disclaimer; another turns a requested life-story analogy into project history. The supplied fairy, St. Paul, unsupported-supernatural and clinically-impossible phrases were not literal matches in training messages. These observations support identity overgeneralization as a hypothesis, not a causal attribution to individual rows.

The next evaluation should compare v0.1 and v0.1.1 under identical templates, system prompts and decoding settings on creative writing, role-play, ordinary editing and unrelated multi-turn tasks. It should separately score task completion, unsolicited identity assertions and inappropriate refusals. Candidate interventions to evaluate include ordinary task-completion targets without identity disclaimers, failure-specific contrast cases, and a base-model behavior-preservation control; expanding identity-only coverage is insufficient. The user example should become a regression case, with separate unseen variants for evaluation.

comments.body:
🤖 Triage: this is an experiment follow-up, with no isolated repository defect to fix. V19 improves identity on the development panel but fails the math preservation check; the same panel guided data expansion, so it cannot establish generalization.

Proposed next experiment:
1. Freeze the v0.1, V13, and V19 model, dataset, template, and scoring revisions. Reserve a new single-turn and delayed-turn identity holdout before further data edits, and score all three checkpoints blind to checkpoint identity under the same rubric, with human review of disputed answers; keep the existing 60 questions development-only.
2. Pre-register promotion gates against both v0.1 and V13 for matched MATH500, GSM8K, and coding evaluations. Include a broader coding set than the 14-task panel, retain per-item traces and fixed denominators, and use the full [Marin eval policy](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10197) panel for any major public release.
3. Run a matched 2×2 ablation of V13/V19 data and expert capacity factors 1/4 from the same v0.1 initializer, with learning rate 1e-6, equal token budgets, and evaluation at steps 25, 50, and 60. Compare paired item outcomes and validation loss to isolate the effects confounded in V19; stop arms that repeat the validation deterioration.
4. Promote only a checkpoint that passes the pre-registered held-out identity and capability gates. Keep v0.1.1 as the accepted release until then. Reuse the pinned-artifact and paired-scoring conventions in [#10409](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10409) and [#10459](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10459) where they fit, without duplicating their training loop.

🤖 **OPD follow-up: shelving this transfer recipe after behavioral validation.** We tried to transfer v0.1.1's identity knowledge into v0.1 while preserving ordinary assistant behavior. Reference identity likelihood improved, but the four students tested with direct generation did not learn to give the correct name or creator; increased identity exposure also raised preservation NLL. This is a negative result for the tested recipe and training budgets, not evidence that OPD cannot work.

We completed five 20-step identity/base mixture arms (0, 16, 32, 48, or 64 identity trajectories per 64) and four 20-step masking arms at 32/32 (control, special-token masking, mask plus frozen embedding/output rows, and identity-span masking). We verified exported-weight changes and the special-row freeze, so this was not simply a no-op training pipeline. The runs use one rollout per input and teacher log-probability feedback. Each arm has one run; small differences between arms are exploratory.

![Corrected validation tradeoffs and recorded manual evaluations](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-OPD-Results/resolve/030681b21f209a15960e9958886320a495dd6589/analysis/heldout-validation-v2/tradeoffs.png)

The plot uses identical corrected development references: 62 held-out SFT identity examples, 99 archived base-model general responses, and 51 base-model initial SWE actions. Lower is better on both axes. SWE initial-action NLL is **not** an end-to-end task-success measure. Labels show nonthinking identity reviews by Codex, not independent humans.

The target is “Marin Snowball”, created by “Open Athena” (also accepting “Open-Athena”). Clean identity means a responsive final answer without material factual errors, unsupported claims, contradictions or omissions; the 12 direct questions are included in the 60. Identity NLL averages response-token loss within each reference, then averages the 62 identity references equally across both modes. Ratio32 and masking control are separate 32/32 runs with differing runtime/callback snapshots; use the masking control for within-round comparisons. The 24 contrastive cases comprise 14 name and 10 creator probes in nonthinking mode; a win requires the best accepted phrase to exceed the strongest listed wrong phrase in summed log probability.

| Model | Corrected identity NLL | Clean identity, thinking off / on | Direct name/creator, thinking off / on |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| Base v0.1 | 3.075 | 6/60; 5/60 | 0/12; 0/12 |
| Teacher v0.1.1 | 0.979 | 49/60; 54/60 | 12/12; 12/12 |
| ratio16 | 2.427 | 4/60; 1/60 | 0/12; 0/12 |
| ratio32 | 2.308 | 5/60; 3/60 | 0/12; 0/12 |
| ratio64 | 2.264 | 3/60; 1/60 | 0/12; 0/12 |
| special-mask | 2.273 | 5/60; 2/60 | 0/12; 0/12 |

The 12-question direct panel is a selected development diagnostic, not an untouched benchmark. Reviews were unblinded; small differences in the broader clean-answer score should not be treated as reliable rankings. Base/teacher values above are fresh matched reruns, distinct from the original SFT-era scores in the issue body.

**What we learned and repaired:** the original OPD validation inserted the same artificial reasoning sentence into every thinking reference. That confounded the signal and invalidated the earlier preservation interpretation and convergence projections. We rebuilt the references, rescored all nine ablation checkpoints plus base and teacher, checked native-template agreement in both modes, and collected 480 new responses alongside 240 existing matched student responses. We also corrected manual-review errors where system-supplied dates had been treated as unsupported claims.

The corrected NLL improvement is real but insufficient: ratio16's nonthinking model-name NLL barely changes, **8.397 → 8.346**, despite aggregate identity NLL improving **3.075 → 2.427**. All four students lose all 24 fixed-prefix name/creator comparisons; the teacher wins all 24. For example, after “I was created by Open”, ratio32 still strongly prefers “AI” over “ Athena”. Shared tokens and surrounding prose can become more likely without fixing the decisive identity choice. These contrastive cases overlap the direct panel and are diagnostic evidence, not an independent replication.

We shelved the recipe because the measured optimization progress did not translate into the intended behavior, while preservation references showed drift. The teacher's known fiction refusals and unsolicited identity assertions also make broad imitation undesirable. The next planned experiment is teacher-assisted mixed-policy GRPO with AI feedback: detect incorrect self-attribution, branch before it, retain the original continuation, obtain a teacher-guided repair for that turn, and learn from rewards using explicit off-policy importance regularization. Later turns return to the student. This GRPO work is planned, not launched.

**Reusable public artifacts:**

- [OPD training pools and corrected validation](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-OPD-Identity): public with automatic gated access, consistent with the SFT dataset. Includes the exact **8,590-row used prompt pool**, a separately labeled **8,666-row candidate expansion**, and **212 corrected development references**, in JSONL and Parquet with hashes. Both training pools are balanced by thinking mode; they overlap and should not be concatenated. These are rollout contexts, not fixed teacher-answer SFT targets. Validation must remain separate from training.
- [Public results archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-OPD-Results): the plot, [detailed audit](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-OPD-Results/blob/030681b21f209a15960e9958886320a495dd6589/VALIDATION_REPAIR_REPORT.md), corrected tables, token-level probes, manual judgments and exact nine run configurations. Historical configs retain the obsolete validation settings and are provenance, not recommended launch recipes.
- [Original V13/V19 SFT dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-Identity-SFT) and [OPD W&B project](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/opd-identity-patch).

The campaign also produced upstream candidates for compacted Megatron token scoring, selected-checkpoint export consistency, explicit scheduler horizons, per-example thinking options and delayed checkpoint saves. Those changes have been identified for extraction; this update does not claim they have been merged.

For scale, general-preservation NLL rose from **0.273** for base to **0.451** for ratio32 and **0.886** for ratio64; SWE initial-action NLL rose from **0.384** to **0.467** and **0.630**, respectively. These are reference-likelihood changes, not measured task-success declines. The teacher’s creative-writing failure is documented in the [revised release assessment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10491); see the section titled “Release assessment revised: creative-writing regression” in the issue body.

Publication revisions: [dataset `52423dfb2b54`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-OPD-Identity/tree/52423dfb2b54d89519860b22bf5625f31220d7c0), [results `030681b21f20`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/open-athena/Marin-Snowball-OPD-Results/tree/030681b21f209a15960e9958886320a495dd6589).

FYI @karansag another "L" in the column for OPD

I think that perhaps part of the problem here is that the initial probability the model assigns to its own name is extremely low; there's very little for OPD to sharpen

Going to tag you with a couple of small PRs I found as a result of this

🤖 @penfever — preparing the owner's requested parallel experiment: a very small direct-identity cold-start SFT from v0.1 (`adc0078a`), with base-answer preservation rows, followed by your 20-step **masking-control** OPD recipe. No GPU runs launched yet.

I will keep this isolated from your planned GRPO work (separate worktree, jobs, caches and output prefixes), use the pinned used prompt pool rather than concatenate the candidate expansion, and replace historical validation with the corrected 212 references. Before reusing/adapting your scripts: which current training/export/scoring scripts and runtime revision should I use, and what GPU layout / observed wall time did the masking-control arm need? Please flag any shared services or resources to avoid. Also want to confirm the precise 24-contrastive/name-span NLL scorer and the matching 12/60-panel artifacts.

The cold start will not put identity assertions into unrelated tasks; the fiction/editing regressions and unseen variants remain evaluation-only. I will report this as a separate cold-start intervention, not a replication of the original zero-cold-start OPD result.

topics.body:
Preserve authoritative FP32 routing-control bias when exporting learned weights in BF16. Frozen short-convolution weights now use an activation-only backward, avoiding saved primal activations and unused weight-gradient buffers. Include GB200 in Fray's device variants, as already used by native sampling.

Focused CPU validation passed 70 cases; 37 hardware-only cases skipped. Accelerator execution was not rerun for this extraction. Existing joint-gradient tolerances are retained.

The averaging, donor initialization, compact SFT, fixed rollout panel and unqualified follow-up paths are preserved with their full source history in [logbooks #2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/issues/2). Two fresh reviewers selected only these existing interfaces for continued Marin maintenance. Supersedes the broad reproduction PR #10539.

Part of #10428.

comments.body: 🤖 Extracted-tree validation: 70 focused CPU tests passed, 37 hardware-only cases skipped; required formatting/type checks passed; the fresh lint-catalog review found no findings. The safe affected suite finished with 2,967 passed, 43 skipped and six expected failures. Its two failures both reproduced on clean unchanged main: offline mode prevented a fixture's loopback wheel download, and the local bubblewrap backend requires Linux. Rerunning the wheel fixture with offline mode unset passed. No source changes were made to bypass either failure. Accelerator execution remains for the declared hardware CI coverage.

🤖 CI is blocked by [taskforge-unit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/39909748946/job/120269935016). Its exact same 11 failing agent-test cases reproduce from a clean checkout of base main `86fc7b67c921ad4ac124835ca7379b04ffa1be25`, using the full Taskforge/capability-environment test selection: 11 failed, 198 passed. Imports were verified against that unchanged checkout. The first failure is the same scripted-model `IndexError: tuple index out of range`; the remaining failures have matching missing-result assertions. Taskforge, RolloutEngine, Shellbox, TaskCompendium and the lockfile are byte-identical between this PR and base main.

The recent green main CI run skipped Taskforge, so it did not establish that this suite passed. Marin, Fray, Levanter and Zephyr unit checks, Levanter TPU/Torch checks, lint and CodeQL passed on this PR. The aggregate unit-tests check remains red because of Taskforge. No test expectations or unrelated source were changed.

topics.body:
## TL;DR

Adjusted WSM-inspired checkpoint averaging → donor initialization of five chat-token output columns → 64 updates of LoRA plus vocabulary SFT produced a provisional Hero checkpoint for short RL capacity-planning trials. All 100 reviewed responses ended at EOT within the 2,048-token cap. Content errors and two special-token anomalies remain; intended-backend throughput and parity still need measurement.

The canonical research record has moved to [marin-logbooks #2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/issues/2), following the workflow in [#9467](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9467). Its [commit-pinned notebook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/d152151d8148734c8f1a954be1224eb83e20c2e9/logbooks/2-hero-checkpoint-format-sft/notebook.md) preserves the full rationale, derivation, source revisions, commands, failed attempts and results. Future research updates belong there. This issue retains the checkpoint handoff and links to the selected Marin contribution.

## What we tried and why

The goal was basic coherent thinking and turn-taking for systems experiments without waiting for a separate full-model cooldown or full-model SFT. Hero is a roughly 535B MoE: 48 layers, hidden width 6,144, 384 routed experts with eight selected per token and two shared experts. This campaign retained its 16K architecture. A is the original pretraining checkpoint at step 294000.

1. **A → B, adjusted averaging.** Inspired by [Warmup-Stable and Merge (WSM)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.17634), divide the integrated target linear-cooldown LR by the integrated actual LR over each saved checkpoint interval. This gave weights 0.232123642 / 0.499105160 / 0.268771198 on steps 282000 / 288000 / 294000. Preserve the latest effective FP32 router bias. This is an offline approximation; no counterfactual optimizer trajectory was run.
2. **B → C, chat-token initialization.** Seed five output columns for header/thinking/EOT tokens from existing text/EOS donor tokens. Input embeddings initially stayed unchanged. Construction and ancestry were verified; no donor/no-donor ablation was run.
3. **C → D, compact SFT.** Freeze the base and routing control; train rank-16/alpha-16 [LoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685) on attention/shared dense projections plus five input/output vocabulary deltas. Use 4,806 no_robots training conversations, the shared Marin chat recipe and pinned tokenizer. Continue an eight-update smoke to 64 total with full Adam, counters and deterministic data position retained. Extending the LR horizon from 8 to 64 raised the first resumed LR from the short tail; it was not a schedule reset. Export ordinary BF16 weights with the deltas baked in.

## How we measured it

| Measurement | Result and scope |
| --- | --- |
| Matched A/B pretraining loss | Identical 59 C4 sequences of 16,384 tokens: 2.130703034 → 2.109083774 (−1.01465%); all 59 row deltas lower. One fixed panel, not broad-domain quality or cooldown equivalence. |
| Training-source EOT acquisition | Mean NLL for one expected EOT token at each of 16 fixed training prefixes: 3.38140 at update 8 → 0.42875 at 64; top-1 1/16 → 14/16. This is EOT-token NLL, not average sequence NLL or heldout evidence. |
| Fresh responses | 40 math, 40 Python and 20 fixed-history followups at temperature 0.7. All 100 stopped at EOT; zero caps; median 113.5 tokens, max 496. Math: 33 correct, four wrong, two incomplete, one ambiguous; code: 32 statically plausible, eight defects; history: 18 clear passes, one error, one borderline. Code was not executed. |

Training processed 67,108,864 positions, including 65,975,980 non-padding tokens: about 47.6 training-corpus token-volume equivalents. This reuse limits interpretation of acquisition gains. Capacity-overflow endpoints were 0.17389 at update 8 and 0.19403 at 64 on different batches; their quality impact is unassessed.

The [reviewed-output gist](https://gist.github.com/dlwh/408759a8eb09796d253b8b53a43769d4) retains every prompt, response and per-case judgment. Native sampling used dropless execution, full-prefix recomputation without KV cache and 4,096 physical padding. Its timing is not an RL-serving throughput measurement. Full heldout/native format/content evaluation, independent merge parity, post-SFT matched C4 regression, long-context behavior and backend agreement remain unresolved.

## Checkpoint artifacts


The merged step-64 native checkpoint contains the LoRA and vocabulary updates baked into ordinary BF16 weights. It needs no runtime adapter:

```text
s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-format-sft/2026.10.21/sft-phase-2416e9d7/SFT-long-test-v1-20261022/attempts/c77824dfce148a77/export/step-64
```

Canonical metadata digest: `aeec732ddaa4d47d146b0056b5b52891e5062a24a61857c35bb48f7e72cdfe57`.

The separate compact checkpoint retains adapters, five vocabulary deltas, full Adam state, counters and deterministic data position for training continuation:

```text
s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-format-sft/2026.10.21/sft-phase-2416e9d7/SFT-long-test-v1-20261022/attempts/c77824dfce148a77/adapters/step-64
```

Canonical metadata digest: `ce7a80fe9c7621e53d3f7745189a523473d7e228eb671a43039396924ae25fb6`.

Use `marin-community/marin-tokenizer` at revision `a5ca45f2feb6c959bd87b81689aa7279b5bdcaa2`, the shared MARIN chat template, and EOT token `128009`. Intended-backend loading and parity still need measurement.

## Status and contribution

[Marin #10556](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10556) retains the independently selected existing-interface fixes: activation-only short-convolution gradients for frozen weights, FP32 router-bias preservation during export and GB200 device typing. The [selection record](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/blob/d152151d8148734c8f1a954be1224eb83e20c2e9/logbooks/2-hero-checkpoint-format-sft/selection.md) explains why the rest stays in the runnable research branch. The broad reproduction PR #10539 is superseded.

Next: load the merged checkpoint on the intended RL backend and measure throughput, latency and memory with representative lengths/concurrency and tokenizer/template/EOT checks. No further training, production adoption or merge is implied.

The [previous attempt](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10428#issuecomment-6334078993) failed with a CUDA illegal-address error at the first compiled gradient execution, before completing an update. The recovery restores the ragged device kernel, symmetric collective buffers and serialized collective overlap; live execution is still needed to establish whether this resolves the failure.

Further diagnosed recovery attempts are authorized within the same eight-update scope. Logs, checkpoint metadata and reports will be retained for each attempt. Completion still requires finite loss and gradients, verified optimizer state, and routing and training-source token-acquisition measurements. A larger pilot and production model deployment remain outside this run’s scope.

🤖 The recovery has completed and saved its first of eight updates on 64 GPUs. Loss was 1.81646 and gradient norm 1.64215. It processed 1,048,576 token positions with 662,639 supervised tokens. The optimizer audit found only the expected trainable parameters and Adam state, with matching shapes, dtypes and byte counts. The permanent checkpoint metadata hash matches the checkpoint telemetry record.

This passes the execution point where the previous attempt crashed. It does not establish the CUDA error’s root cause or complete the eight-update smoke. It retains the same data, learning rates and 64-GPU topology and will run the seven remaining updates to reach eight total. 🤖 The diagnostic continuation restored Adam at step 1 and completed update 2 (loss 1.81864, gradient norm 1.66488), then hit the same NCCL invalid-argument error on its next gradient. A matching [prior diagnosis](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8861#issuecomment-5531532861) describes an evaluation executable with shorter sequences registering a smaller overlapping collective-memory window, breaking the subsequent training executable.

A repaired continuation is submitted from the saved second checkpoint for six remaining updates, reaching eight total. Acquisition measurements now restore each update’s compact checkpoint after all gradient updates finish. Core telemetry and a queue of pending measurements, bound to those telemetry bytes by SHA256, preserve unfinished work across interruptions and resumes with no updates left. Data, model, optimizer state and schedule are unchanged.

All 114 safe Hero tests pass, including restoration of exact saved adapter parameters and Adam/counter state after interrupted diagnostics; scoped lint passes and type checking reports zero errors. GPU verification of the repair remains pending. Acquisition measures end-of-turn token top-1 accuracy and NLL on 16 fixed training-source prefixes; heldout format/content quality remains unmeasured.

🤖 The eight-update SFT smoke completed. All 64 GPU processes exited successfully. Final compact/native metadata hashes match the recorded checkpoint and handoff digests; model arrays were not independently read back. Continuations restored saved Adam state at steps 1 and 2, preserving counters and deterministic data position. No native preemption occurred. Moving acquisition evaluations after the gradient loop allowed the six remaining updates and their saved-state diagnostics to finish.

The campaign executed 8,388,608 token positions, including 8,252,608 non-padding and 5,314,600 supervised tokens. Training loss went from 1.81646 to 1.70861 across different packed batches. On 16 fixed training-source prefixes, end-of-turn token NLL fell from 9.82290 to 3.38140 and top-1 matches rose from 0/16 to 1/16. Losses and gradients were finite for all eight updates, and selected input-embedding vocabulary deltas had nonzero gradients throughout.

Routing measurements are available for updates 3–8: mean capacity-overflow rate changed from 0.18325 to 0.17389. Its quality impact has not been assessed. Compact Adam audits passed initially and after both stateful recoveries. Independent measurement review passed 68 checks; source validation passed 114 safe Hero tests and type/lint checks.

Next are heldout format/content evaluation, the original pretraining baseline’s full native format/content suite, and numerical comparison of the adapter-equipped model with its merged native export. The measurements span three execution segments; `format_eval assemble-smoke` currently requires one execution and optimizer step zero, so segment-aware aggregation is needed before using this campaign to qualify a larger pilot. No larger pilot or production deployment was launched.

🤖 A separately authorized longer LoRA-plus-vocabulary SFT test is submitted, continuing the completed eight-update smoke to 64 total updates on 64 GPUs. It adds at most 56 updates and caps cumulative non-padding tokens at 67,108,864; it stops before an update that would exceed the cap. Rank 16/alpha 16, the five vocabulary-token deltas, global batch of 64 sequences × 16,384 positions, training data and peak learning rates (LoRA 1e-4; vocabulary 1e-5) remain fixed.

The request pins restoration of the full compact Adam state, parameters, counters and deterministic data position at update 8. The finite linear learning-rate schedule now ends at update 64; the first resumed update uses about 90.3% of the peak rates. This raises the learning rate from the earlier smoke's short cooldown tail, without restarting warmup or counters. Every update saves a compact checkpoint. Fixed training-source end-of-turn diagnostics run after the gradient sequence to avoid the previously observed train/eval collective failure. Actual restoration and further learning remain to be verified.

This test measures whether further updates improve token acquisition and remain numerically stable. Heldout formatting/content quality, adapter-versus-merged parity and the original pretraining baseline's full format/content suite remain unresolved. The earlier smoke spans three execution segments; its single-execution qualification remains unresolved. Results and exact token/update accounting will follow here.

🤖 The 64-update LoRA-plus-vocabulary SFT test completed. The continuation's 64 GPU processes exited successfully, with no application failures or preemptions. It restored full compact Adam state, parameters, counters and deterministic data position at step 8, then ran 56 new updates under the reviewed 64-update learning-rate schedule.

On the same 16 fixed training-source prefixes:

| Update | EOT token NLL | Top-1 EOT matches |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 8 | 3.38140 | 1/16 |
| 16 | 1.35890 | 12/16 |
| 32 | 0.65719 | 13/16 |
| 48 | 0.46985 | 14/16 |
| 64 | 0.42875 | 14/16 |

Each prefix scores one EOT target token. These are training-source acquisition diagnostics; heldout generation and turn termination remain unmeasured. Supervised training loss changed from 1.70861 at step 8 to 1.63851 at step 64 across different packed batches. All 56 new updates had finite losses, gradients and routing measurements. The joint gradient norm of the five selected input-embedding vocabulary deltas was nonzero at every new update. Mean capacity-overflow rate rose from 0.17389 at step 8 to 0.19403 at step 64; its quality impact is unassessed.

The campaign executed 67,108,864 token positions, including 65,975,980 non-padding and 42,664,754 assistant-supervised tokens. Final compact/native checkpoint and handoff metadata hashes match their recorded identities; model arrays were not independently read back. Audits confirmed compact Adam state and returned gradients for only the intended adapter and vocabulary parameters. Independent review passed 529 checks with no findings. The continuation took 29m53s; median steady update time was 2.681s and median compact-checkpoint time was 22.52s.

Next are heldout EOT/format/content evaluation and numerical adapter-versus-merged parity. The original pretraining baseline's full native format/content suite remains incomplete. The campaign preserves four execution segments and the 8-to-64 schedule change; `format_eval assemble-smoke` still assumes one execution starting with fresh Adam and was not used to qualify this campaign. No further training extension or serving adoption was launched.

🤖 A 100-rollout generation sanity check is submitted for a provisional capacity-planning handoff of the merged step-64 SFT checkpoint. No further training or full-model cooldown is included. The panel contains 40 GSM8K test problems, 40 fresh synthetic Python tasks and 20 synthetic follow-ups with fixed conversation histories. None of the selected prompts exactly matches normalized SFT train/heldout prompts; pretraining contamination remains unknown. Each case generates one assistant reply using the shared Marin chat template, temperature 0.7, a 2,048-token cap and EOT stopping.

Raw tokens and transcripts will be retained. Results will cover turn termination, invented user turns, repetition, token-limit hits and response lengths, with qualitative review of basic reasoning, code plausibility and context-following. Generated code will not be executed. Cap hits count as unfinished, separately from broken turn-taking; coherent responses still reasoning at the cutoff may need a small targeted longer-cap follow-up.

The existing native BF16 sampler uses dropless inference routing and uncached full-prefix forward passes. It pads to 4,096 positions on a 16K-capable model; every prompt plus its generation cap fits that physical window. This checks response usability and lengths. Its timing is not a serving or RL throughput estimate; capacity numbers still require measurements in the intended runtime.

🤖 The first 100-rollout inference submission was rejected before any tasks started because storage credentials were not forwarded. No model evaluation ran. The terminal evidence is preserved, and a recovery submission is being prepared with the same checkpoint, prompts and generation limits. Responses that reach the 2,048-token cap will be reported as unfinished, separately from role leakage or malformed turn-taking.

🤖 The corrected 100-rollout check has been submitted using an updated submission client. The checkpoint, prompts and generation settings are unchanged. Actual execution and model outputs are still pending. The earlier rejected submission ran no model evaluation. We will inspect every response for basic reasoning, history-following, turn-taking and repetition, and report token-cap truncation separately. This remains a provisional checkpoint sanity check for RL capacity planning; native sampler timing does not measure serving throughput.

🤖 The corrected 100-rollout check now has all 16 tasks running, with zero failures or preemptions. A credential-protocol mismatch rejected the two earlier submissions before model evaluation. The checkpoint, prompts and generation settings are unchanged: temperature 0.7 and a 2,048-token cap. GPU process initialization, checkpoint restore and generated outputs remain to be verified. The review will cover all responses and separate token-cap truncation from broken turn-taking. Native sampler timing remains outside the serving-throughput claim.

🤖 Preliminary review of the first 64 saved rollouts: all 64 ended with EOT, with zero 2,048-token cap hits; output lengths were 10–496 tokens. Of 26 math cases, 23 were correct, one wrong, one incomplete and one ungraded because the reference was ambiguous. Of 25 code implementations, 20 appeared plausible on static inspection and five had functional defects; no generated code was executed. Of 13 fixed-history follow-ups, 11 clearly met the request, one lost track of possession, and one had a borderline item-count issue depending on whether drawing supplies count as a kit or separate physical items.

No role continuation or pathological repetition was observed. One correct math reply contained a stray `<|end_think|>` marker. This is a small qualitative panel; review of the remaining 36 responses and final manifest verification are pending. Native sampler timing does not measure serving throughput.

🤖 The 100-rollout sanity check supports using the checkpoint with LoRA and vocabulary deltas merged into ordinary weights provisionally for RL capacity and throughput measurement on the backend chosen by the measurement team. All 100 responses ended with EOT, with zero 2,048-token cap hits; median length was 113.5 tokens and maximum length was 496.

Manual review found 33 correct final math answers, four wrong, two incomplete and one ambiguous reference across 40 cases. One correct final answer contained contradictory reasoning. Of 40 code implementations, 32 appeared plausible on static inspection and eight had functional defects; no generated code was executed. Of 20 fixed-history follow-ups, 18 clearly met the request, one lost track of possession, and one had a borderline item-count issue depending on whether drawing supplies count as a kit or separate physical items.

No literal role continuation or pathological repetition was observed. Two responses had raw special-token anomalies: a stray closing thinking marker, and an end/start-of-text pair before EOT. This supports a provisional systems handoff, with those defects retained in the record. Native sampler timing does not measure serving throughput. Loading on that backend and numerical agreement with the native checkpoint remain unchecked. Complete held-out quality and native format/content evaluations, and long-context behavior, remain unresolved. topics.title: [rigging] fsutil verified-copy cannot promote multipart objects on CoreWeave S3; failed uploads leave truncated staging objects
topics.body:
`fsutil verified-copy` into a CoreWeave S3 bucket cannot finish for any object stored as a multipart upload. The promote step fails with:

```
Error: promoted object does not match verified staging object: model-00001-of-00502.safetensors
```

This is current main: `lib/rigging/src/rigging/fsutil/verified_copy.py` was last changed in e9d42161ab ([#9606](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9606)).

## Cause

`_promote` copies the staged object with `filesystem.cp_file(staging_path, destination_path, preserve_etag=True)`. It then accepts the result only if the new ETag equals the staging ETag recorded in the resume marker (`_destination_matches_marker`, `staging_identity="etag=..."`). s3fs's `preserve_etag` path (`_copy_etag_preserved`) rebuilds the same part layout with `upload_part_copy`.

CoreWeave AI Object Storage gives a multipart object assembled from `UploadPartCopy` parts a different ETag than the same bytes uploaded with `UploadPart`, even when the part sizes are identical. The comparison can never succeed for multipart objects there. Single-part objects keep a plain MD5 ETag and promote fine.

Minimal reproduction against `s3://marin-rno2a` (rigging `filesystem_for`, s3fs 2026.1.0):

| Object (3 parts of 8 MiB + 1 MiB tail, random bytes) | ETag |
|---|---|
| Standard multipart ETag (md5 of part md5s) | `288f9995ba2170a993a398f1a1fcf144-3` |
| After upload (`open(..., "wb", block_size=8 MiB)`) | `288f9995ba2170a993a398f1a1fcf144-3` (matches) |
| After `cp_file(src, dst, preserve_etag=True)` | `55c8602f25d3f874ad13931d9b01d75d-3` (different; bytes identical) |

`head_object(PartNumber=i)` returns correct per-part ranges on CoreWeave: `bytes 0-52428799/656670848`, ..., part 13 `27525248` bytes. So s3fs reproduces the part layout correctly. Only the ETag differs.

## Observed

The copy was `gs://marin-us-central2/scratch/karan/rsi-merge/merges/avg-SC/` → `s3://marin-rno2a/scratch/karan/task289/merges/avg-SC/`, 509 objects, 134 GB, run as Iris jobs `/karan/rsi289-copy-avg-SC` and `/karan/rsi289-copy-avg-SC-r2` (2026-10-24).

- 429 objects promoted. 80 were left in `avg-SC.verified-copy-staging/`. The manifest has exactly 80 objects over the 50 MiB part size, which are the multipart ones.
- Example: `model-00001-of-00502.safetensors`, 656,670,848 bytes. Marker `staging_identity` was `etag=d635d51ef0ed17b23e7a1a0190357b4c-13`; the copied object's ETag was `7217d670f6e2dc4b0cdd681b1dbf9d1e-13`. The sha256 of the copy matches the source.
- The second merge (`ta-S-C-A5`, job `/karan/rsi289-copy-ta-S-C-A5`) shows the same pattern.

## Related: a failed upload leaves a committed partial object in staging

Both copies also died once on `OSError: [Errno 5] An error occurred (408) when calling the UploadPart operation: Request Timeout` (16 workers; 8 workers also hit it). `_copy_with_hash` writes inside `with destination_fs.open(staging_path, "wb", block_size=50 MiB)`. fsspec's `AbstractBufferedFile.__exit__` always calls `close()` → `flush(force=True)`, so s3fs completes the multipart upload with the parts already sent, even while an exception is propagating.

For `ta-S-C-A5`, `model-00140-of-00502.safetensors` and `model-00141-of-00502.safetensors` were left in staging at 209,715,200 bytes each (exactly 4 × 50 MiB) of 1,677,721,760.

verified-copy itself is safe here: no resume marker is written for those objects, and a rerun recopies them. But the staging prefix holds complete-looking objects that are truncated. Anything that reads staging directly gets bad data. A manual finishing step did this, and only a sha256 check against the source manifest caught it.

## Suggested fixes

1. In `_promote` (and in `_destination_matches_marker`), don't rely on ETag equality across a server-side copy for multipart objects. Either:
   - re-hash the promoted object with sha256 when the identity is a multipart ETag (`-N` suffix), or
   - for S3 backends, skip promote and write the final object directly, verifying sha256 on the destination as staging already does.
   Recording `sha256=` instead of `etag=` as the staging identity for multipart objects would also work.
2. In `_copy_with_hash`, abort the upload on error instead of committing it: call `destination.discard()` (s3fs aborts the MPU), or open with `autocommit=False` and `commit()` only after the loop completes. Then a failed copy leaves no object behind.
3. Consider retrying `UploadPart` 408s (`retries` in the s3fs client config). Two 134 GB copies each failed once at 8-16 workers.

## Workaround used

Finish the move in-cluster, then check every object's sha256 and size against the merge's own manifest. Script: `experiments/weight_merging/rsi/screen_289/finish_copy.py` on branch `task/289`. Delete truncated staged objects first and recopy them from the source.

comments.body:
🤖 **Research**

`_promote` requires the copied object's ETag to equal the staging ETag. CoreWeave changes multipart ETags for `UploadPartCopy`, so matching bytes fail promotion. A write error also exits the buffered writer through `close()`, which can complete a truncated multipart upload.

**Relevant code**
- [`verified_copy.py#L413-L421`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/fsutil/verified_copy.py#L413-L421) — promotion and identity check.
- [`verified_copy.py#L427-L449`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/fsutil/verified_copy.py#L427-L449) — staging writer.
- [`verified_copy.py#L469-L476`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/rigging/src/rigging/fsutil/verified_copy.py#L469-L476) — marker comparison.

**Proposed Fix**

Accept a changed multipart ETag only after SHA-256 matches the verified marker, including on resume. Abort a failed staging upload before the writer closes so partial parts cannot become a visible object. Cover both paths with local filesystem fakes; leave 408 retry policy for separate tuning.

🤖 Implementation detail: the S3 writer will use `autocommit=False`. Closing a failed writer can flush parts, but it cannot publish the object; `discard()` then aborts the multipart upload. A successful stream closes and commits explicitly.

🤖 Fix proposed in #10639. Multipart promotions now verify SHA-256 when CoreWeave changes the ETag, and failed S3 staging uploads are discarded before publication. The affected local rigging suites passed (100 tests); live CoreWeave validation has not run.

August 20th: noticed that we are OOMing every ~3 hours.

We attempted interventions to adjust XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.83 (giving XLA more memory). This made things worse. 

--xla_gpu_memory_limit_slop_factor seems to be another promising tunable. Adjusting to 0.88 from the default 0.95 didn't help. Testing with 0.85 now.

We observed periodic host OOMs after several checkpoints. https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/200 . Restarting with the following changes:

1. Tensorstore restore parallelism bounded by a fixed budget
2. Checkpoint offload cache to 16GB
3. malloc_trim() calls after each checkpoint

in theory 2 will make checkpoints faster (fully async), and 3 will prevent the host OOM recurrence

`malloc_trim` was still inconsistently resulting in OOMs during checkpointing. Restarting on main with the jemalloc changes in.

Restores were hitting single worker stalls. Merged and running with #8584 . First restore after this change was successful, though it might have been luck/caching.

🤖 Relaunched after a checkpoint-time OOM

The `coord-fast-restore` instance OOMed while saving step 11252 at 22:57 UTC. Iris retried the 176-task child, so the root was cancelled to avoid overlapping production gangs.

Replacement: https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Fpower%2Fhero-12d8b6f0-dee637-coord-memfix

The replacement uses `main` at `8aaeb40fe2dd152734801edafe474f8e52ef78f8`, the existing `hero-12d8b6f0-dee637` run ID, size `d6144`, version `2026.08.19.2`, and the existing W&B/output lineage. The launcher will select the newest complete checkpoint. The coordinator uses JAX port `32615`.

🤖 Memory sampling on the current `coord-memfix` instance isolates checkpoint-correlated retained RSS to writer tasks 0–127. Their median floor rose 11.7 GiB after the first save and 4.4 GiB after the second; tasks 128–175 stayed on the baseline slope. Each writer rank was assigned about 9.5–10.2 GiB, and `/proc` attributes the retained difference to anonymous memory across the four child Python processes.

The run contains #8609. The signature matches its documented persistent CUDA pinned-host BFC pool cost. The smaller second increment does not support projecting a fixed 30 GiB leak per save.

Incident record: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/227

🤖 Correction after tracing the current checkpoint path: the long-lived `GlobalAsyncCheckpointManager` keeps the completed TensorStore commit futures in `_commit_futures`; `wait_until_finished()` joins but does not clear them, and the writes allow indefinite source-buffer references. This mechanism predates #8609 and plausibly retains one staged checkpoint share per writer rank. PR #8599 contained a reviewed post-join cleanup for these futures, but that part did not land with #8609. The pinned-host BFC pool in #8609 remains an additional allocator-level floor that clearing the manager cannot purge. Updated evidence and safe cleanup boundaries: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/227

🤖 At 08:52:52 UTC, training task 8 OOMed during checkpoint serialization. The 2 GB coordinator OOMed 16 seconds later. Its zero failure retry budget then stopped the 176-task child job.

On two trays with the Harrier mixture, global batch 1024, and sequence length 4096, the profiler-free 1 GB/process arm delivered 0.937 batches/s including cold start versus 0.956 batches/s at 125 GB/process. The hero runs at 19.9 s/step (0.050 batches/s), so the 1 GB cap has 18.6x headroom and bounds the decoded cache near 0.923 GiB/process. Report: https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/235

🤖 Attempt 0 failed after node `s6htxs64` lost connectivity. At 16:53:31 UTC, JAX reported that process IDs 333–335 had stopped sending heartbeats; startup logs map those IDs to local ranks 1–3 of Iris task 83 on that node. Kubernetes marked the node `NotReady` 11 seconds later, CoreWeave cordoned it for `ConnectivityUpdateTime`, and the node rebooted at 17:07. topics.title: [iris] Deliver application secrets through files
topics.head: de921e221f4338c27758b1725cde691d82ecfe4f
topics.body:
Deliver application secrets through per-attempt VM tmpfs files and Pod-owned Kubernetes Secrets. Rigging provides named file-first lookup with environment fallback and shared native HF and AWS file discovery. Submissions automatically include the client's current mounted bundle and available HF/W&B/CoreWeave credentials from files or environment fallback. Explicit entries override inherited defaults. Other credentials use the secrets map or CLI `--secret NAME SOURCE`.

The submitting client resolves inheritance for ordinary child jobs, Fray actors and Zephyr workers. `SecretBehavior.ISOLATE` and sandboxes send only explicit secrets. The controller receives the resolved map for dispatch and retries. Remove cluster default application credentials and operator environment injection. Ordinary `env_vars` retain environment delivery.

CoreWeave tasks require the submitter's own storage keys, delivered through the same bundle with native AWS file discovery. Their output uploader receives only a native AWS file containing the submitted storage keys. Operator storage keys remain restricted to infrastructure Pods. Development callers of `configure_coreweave_s3()` must supply native AWS credential configuration explicitly; it no longer exports credential values into the process environment. Controller signing credentials remain controller-only. Submitted values still travel through authenticated job RPCs and remain in database/checkpoint state; display APIs redact every secret-map value.

Apply the IaC namespace Role/RoleBinding for per-attempt Secrets before deploying the Kubernetes controller. The `cw-us-west-04a` stack must first import CI's bootstrapped `task-secret-role` and `task-secret-binding` resources into Pulumi state, following the linked deployment guide. Update submitters and runtime images together, and roll GCP workers for new attempts to use files. Existing containers retain their original delivery. No new HF/W&B cloud resources or grants are required. See the [secret-delivery guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/weaver/rigging-secret-management/lib/iris/docs/secrets.md) for configuration, deployment and rotation.

Rollout incident: [CoreWeave submission failures during secret-file cutover](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/838).

🤖 Holistic review of `204b6bbab639e2c3378943e4c48b557a0a910952`: **one blocker**.

This change moves application credentials from automatic task environment injection to a submitted secret map. The controller persists that map and resolves child inheritance from the authorized parent job. VM workers mount per-attempt tmpfs files; Kubernetes tasks mount a Pod-owned Secret. Rigging supplies file-first reads, and job status redacts secret values. Trusted CoreWeave tasks still receive a separate storage credential mount.

The [Iris unit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/39811072686/job/119940659922) and [Rigging unit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/39811072686/job/119940659342) checks passed at this head. The [SkyRL wheel check](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/39811072686/job/119940658579) failed; the CoreWeave CI test was still running when I reviewed it. I found no live rollout evidence in this PR.

**Findings**

- **1. Blocker:** [environment_contract.py:21](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/204b6bbab639e2c3378943e4c48b557a0a910952/vendor/skyrl/marinskyrl/environment_contract.py#L21) imports Rigging when the module loads. [bootstrap_runtime.sh:63](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/204b6bbab639e2c3378943e4c48b557a0a910952/vendor/skyrl/cloud/iris/bootstrap_runtime.sh#L63) executes that module even when it never reads a credential. The wheel check's minimal bootstrap runtimes lack Rigging, so 11 bootstrap tests stop at `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'rigging'` before their intended checks. Move the Rigging import into `application_secret()`, where the runtime credential lookup actually needs it, and rerun `skyrl-wheel`.

- **2. Related PR:** [tasks.py:959](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/204b6bbab639e2c3378943e4c48b557a0a910952/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/backends/k8s/tasks.py#L959) mounts shared storage credentials into trusted task Pods, while [#10475](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10475) removes that mount and requires submitter storage keys in task environments. These branches define conflicting CoreWeave task credential contracts. Merge this PR first, then rebase #10475 onto it and reconcile the storage mount, submitter validation, and output uploader together before deploying either controller change.

- **3. Related PR:** [client.py:1026](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/204b6bbab639e2c3378943e4c48b557a0a910952/lib/iris/src/iris/client/client.py#L1026) rebuilds `EnvironmentSpec` for children. [#9999](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9999) adds an explicit child environment mode to this same path and uses `dataclasses.replace` to retain fields. Merge this PR first, then rebase #9999 and preserve both its explicit environment mode and this PR's secret map and `SecretBehavior` in the combined client path.

🤖 Yes, for a `marin`/`cw-*` pair running the updated controllers. The submitting client resolves the secret map before submission. `marin` stores the full environment, including `secrets`, in its job config; pending handoffs reconstruct that environment from storage. The [handoff builder](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/de921e221f4338c27758b1725cde691d82ecfe4f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/federation/manager.py#L461) copies the full `LaunchJobRequest` and removes only the cluster routing constraint. The CW peer stores the received map and [rebuilds it for task dispatch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/de921e221f4338c27758b1725cde691d82ecfe4f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/projections/run_templates.py#L75). Retries use that stored map.

`FederationSync` runs from `marin` to the CW peer to fetch status. Its [response](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/de921e221f4338c27758b1725cde691d82ecfe4f/lib/iris/src/iris/rpc/controller.proto#L820) contains job/task deltas and endpoints, with no environment field. The [parent mirror](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/de921e221f4338c27758b1725cde691d82ecfe4f/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/federation_store.py#L287) updates state and task rows; it does not overwrite the root job's stored environment. Children launched on CW resolve inheritance from their mounted bundle there, and sync mirrors their status back.

This requires both controllers, submitters, and task images to understand the new `EnvironmentConfig.secrets` field. There is no mixed-version negotiation; an old controller can lose the map when it persists or dispatches a job. Existing queued jobs without personal CW keys need resubmission. I found no regression test that sends a nonempty secret map through a two-controller handoff, retry, and sync, so this conclusion is from code inspection rather than a live cross-cluster run.

topics.title: [grug] Let the hero launcher run context parallelism
topics.head: 82f2b8d076ef6992159a22c7b9bec5220fc4ce81
topics.body:
The hero's 262K context extension needs context parallelism, and at 65K CP4 with row balancing is faster than CP1 and drops fewer routed tokens, but the production hero launcher (`launch_scaling_ladder.py`, d6144) did not support it: it fixed the expert axis at all 64 GPUs of a rack and had no context axis. Only `launch_diagnostics.py` could run CP. The launcher now can:

- `hero_recipe.py` adds the checked-in constants `HERO_CONTEXT_AXIS_SIZE = 1` and `HERO_BALANCE_ATTENTION_ROWS = False` (#10121's row balancing), so the 65K deploy sets CP4 and row balancing with one line each.
- At CP > 1 each rack's 64 GPUs (`HERO_RACK_GPUS`, formerly `HERO_EP_EXPERT_AXIS_SIZE`) form 64 / CP expert shards, and the Levanter trainer mesh counts only batch shards, as `launch_diagnostics.py` already did.
- The eval batch is one sequence per batch shard: 704 at 16K CP1, 176 at 65K CP4. Both are 11.5M tokens per eval batch and 16,384 tokens per GPU on the dropless eval mesh; holding 704 at 65K CP4 would quadruple the per-GPU load.
- Both launchers share one launch-time check that the batch, `max_seq_len` and the expert bank split over the layout. `launch_diagnostics.py` defaults its context axis and row balancing to the hero constants.
- The loader logs each source's start offset at a context switch.

The 16K hero is unchanged: its full built config (trainer, mesh, eval, model, optimizer) has the same repr as on the merge base, and a test pins its layout.

Part of #8435

The production hero launcher (`launch_scaling_ladder.py`, d6144) can now run context parallelism. `hero_recipe.py` holds the hero's context-parallel degree and row-balancing switch as checked-in constants, `HERO_CONTEXT_AXIS_SIZE = 1` and `HERO_BALANCE_ATTENTION_ROWS = False`, so the 65K deploy sets CP4 and #10121's row balancing with one line each. Complete ordered source manifests, upstream locator backfill, historical transform provenance, and full-store count reconciliation remain unfinished. Frozen Harrier provenance was recovered for 291 sources; Common Crawl Focus remains unresolved, and selected-document embedding coverage is unmeasured.

The affected safe test suite passed 64 tests, mechanical lint passed, and the strict documentation build passed.

topics.title: [grug] Balance attention work across batch shards in hero train step
topics.head: 4268f15cf5b942b78bac5c3fee362b9f860f0cdf
topics.body:
The hero train step can now permute the rows of each global batch so that each batch shard gets a similar amount of attention work. It is off by default and runs only when `GrugTrainerConfig.balance_attention_rows` is set; the diagnostics launcher exposes it as `--balance-attention-rows`. Document packing gives rows very different attention costs, and every layer waits for the busiest shard at its next collective. On real 16K hero batches, the busiest of 64 shards did 2.10x the mean global-attention work.

`balance_attention_rows` counts each row's attended query-key pairs from its FA4 segment bounds and excludes padding. It sorts the rows by this count and deals them to the batch shards in snake order. Each shard keeps its rows in loader order. Expert capacity drops a shard's later tokens first, and the mixture loader shuffles rows within a batch, so loader order spreads drops over rows of all costs. A cost order within a shard would drop short-document rows first. A full receiver keeps earlier senders' tokens first, so the deal starts at the shard the costliest row was loaded on rather than at shard 0. Context ranks share rows, so the shard count excludes the context axis. With one row per shard, as in the 262K CP4 layout, placement cannot change any shard's work, so the batch is returned unchanged. The count is at token granularity. FA4 skips whole 128x128 tiles, so rows of short documents cost somewhat more than counted. With this count, the busiest-to-mean ratio at 16K falls from 2.10 to 1.17 for global layers and from 1.46 to 1.05 for local layers. These ratios were computed before padding was excluded from the count.

Every token still enters the loss and the router statistics. Row placement changes which assignments exceed expert capacity, so the loss changes slightly.

Each pair of arms ran on one GB200 NVL72 rack. The step-time change is the median per-step paired difference with a 95% bootstrap interval.

| Context | Mesh and batch | Restored from | Control s/step | Balanced s/step | Step time | Scored steps |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 65K | CP4 x EP16, 64 rows | hero-ctx16k-step257k, step 300000 | 15.352 | 14.743 | -3.63% [-4.02, -2.85] | 106 / 57 |
| 16K | EP64, 256 rows | hero-mfu30-step231k, step 240000 | 13.134 | 13.078 | -0.40% [-0.46, -0.31] | 106 / 106 |

The balanced 65K arm was preempted once, so only 57 steps are paired. The drop fraction rises by about 0.5% at both lengths (ratio 1.006 at 65K, 1.005 at 16K). The only same-code A/A pair is at 16K: its loss difference has an RMS of 4.5e-4 and a maximum of 1.4e-3. The 65K loss difference is inside that band (RMS 2.6e-4, maximum 1.9e-3). The 16K loss difference is above it (RMS 8.3e-4, maximum 5.8e-3, mean +2.8e-4). No 65K A/A pair exists.

The permutation all-gathers the whole global batch to every GPU: 12 bytes per global token for the tokens, the loss weights and the q segment ids, which also serve as the kv ids. At the 11-rack 65K layout of 704 rows, that is about 0.55 GB per GPU per step. The cost of this gather across racks has not been measured. Balancing is therefore opt-in: it gained 3.6% at 65K but only 0.4% at 16K on one rack, and at 16K on 11 racks the gather may cost a large share of that gain. The 65K hero switch is expected to turn it on.

topics.title: [Hero Run] 535B-A23B on 18T tokens
topics.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.
