🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| rung | racks | batch | steps | tokens | active |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |
| d1024 | 2 | 2048 | 15,276 | 128B | 162M |
| d1536 | 6 | 6144 | 15,128 | 381B | 481M |
| d2048 | 11 | 11,264 | 20,072 | 926B | 1.2B |
| **d6144 (hero)** | 11 | 11,264 | 390,139 | **18.0T** | 22.8B |

## 6. Code (at run commit [`12d8b6f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be))

**Model** ([`model.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py)) — [`GrugModelConfig`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L160)
- All-MoE routed FFN: [`MoEMLP`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L907) · shared experts [`DenseMLP`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L637)
- QB routing (histogram estimator): threshold/beta [`_qb_beta_hist`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L874), histogram build [`_histogram_from_expert_counts`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L820), applied next-step as stop-grad bias
- Sigmoid combine + renorm-to-2.5: [`_ROUTING_RENORM_SUM`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L58), [combine](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L980)
- LatentMoE + learnable latent RMSNorm: [`latent_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1046)
- RMSNorm on embeddings/readout: [`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223), [`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1203); [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594)
- GatedNorm: [`GatedNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L612)
- XSA (exclusive self-attention): [subtract V-parallel component](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L573)
- Attention head gate (zero-init): [`attn_gate`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L583)
- RMS qk-norm: [`rms_norm(q)`,`rms_norm(k)`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L534)
- Partial (half) RoPE, fused: [`_rope`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L553), [`rope_fused`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L541); rope-free global layers via per-layer bounds [L1252](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1252)
- ShortConv: [`ShortConv`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L420) → fused Pallas [`short_conv`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L52)
- Attention (FA4-cute): [call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L572), [`fa4_cute_segment_bounds`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1252)
- Untied embeddings: [`token_embed`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1160), [`output_proj`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1163)
- Homogeneous global/local scan (rope diff + GQA diff): [`ArrayStacked` scan body](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1262), rope-free select via [`jnp.where(disable_rope)`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L568), per-layer KV-head [`lax.cond(is_global)`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L521), per-layer mask-bounds [select](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1268)

## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

Comparing our scaling law to prior runs. The main differences here is that the May recipe is at compute optimal, this run is at ~12x overtrained, and the 67B-A2B scaling law was at 100x overtrained. The 67B-A2B ran at 8k seqlen, and was therefore given a lower asympotote of 1.4 instead of 1.5. The May fit also inaccurately has an asympotote at 1.6 instead of 1.5. Main architecture change is we dropped from 4/256 level of sparsity to 4/192 level of sparsity (25% fewer total parameters, to fit on GB200 at this scale. Several other small features added. Overall, the scaling law looks reasonable and nothing looks off in the training dynamics or data. Grad norms look stable over the run, peaking at 25% into the run. These runs ran at oversized batch sizes, which may be slightly suppressing the gradient. Expecting the grad norm to climb higher on the hero run, but still peak at the same ~25% into the run. This will be good metric to monitor for issues. Drop rate jumps to 10 pct at very start, then drops to 0, then climbs to ~4pct over the run. Slightly increasing as we scale. Predicting we wont have that 10 percent spike for the hero, because our warmup (1 percent) will cover a much larger number of steps since the hero is at a higher step count. I think most likely scenario is the hero runs around 2 percent dropping, but up to 8 percent seems plausible bsaed on the data at 4k seqlen.

Also noting- the d2048 scaling ladder rung failed at 81%. Chose not to resume to add more time to Hero Run. The dynamics look clear from the first 81 percent, and we can cleanly extrapolate the last 19%. From a practical perspective, we will not actually be running the end of the run at 4k seqlen, and the datamix may update midrun. So the utility of the scaling law is more around the first 50 percent of the run and ensuring the projection is reasonably within expectation (which it is).

From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. I agree this probably needs larger-scale ablations to judge properly.

🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

I posted an independent, pre-registered forecast of the final dropless Paloma macro, with intervals, in #9977: median 2.035, 80% [2.023, 2.047], using data through step 227,999. That puts the run on track to match or slightly beat the Aug 19 pre-registration. It also traces most of the 2.04 vs 2.10 gap to whether lm_head FLOPs are counted in compute. cc @ClassicLarry @dlwh

**An independent forecast of the final loss, with a law found from the data (no fixed form)**

I forecast the run's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss`: the last eval logged in the lineage at step 387,000 or later, as W&B records it (expected at 16K packing). I used only public W&B data, up to step 302,999 (snapshot of 2026-10-21, 22:58 UTC).

| forecast | data | value | 90 % interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | ladder + the hero's own evals | **1.979** | [1.965, 1.994] |
| B | ladder only | **1.935** | [1.915, 1.963] |

**Method in brief.** NAI, the symbolic-regression system I develop, finds a law L(C, fraction of training) from the table, with no form given: no floor and no power law are assumed. C is your lm_head-excluded compute.
- B is the ladder-only law at the hero's compute and the end of training.
- A adds the hero's post-swap 4K evals to the table and takes the level from its 16 evals at 16K.
- The intervals are NAI's forecast band, nominally 90 %.

B is 0.10 below the Aug 19 pre-registration from the same ladder, because the law NAI found has no fixed floor.

The formulas are sealed. Their SHA-256 digests and the scoring rules, fixed in advance: https://github.com/mindscanlabs/NAI-track-record/blob/main/forecasts/marin-535b.md

I'll post the formulas and the scored comparison after the run ends. Thanks for running this in the open: it makes a forecast like this possible.

A measurement for anyone checking forecasts made while the evals packed at 4K (Marin's Aug 19 forecast of 2.039, and mine in #9977): the switch to 16K lowered the Paloma macro by about 0.031 on nearly the same weights. The `qk16k-a1-step252k` arm restored step 252,000 with the hero's post-switch settings (16K, `qk_mult` 1.48) and logged 2.0929 and 2.0926 at steps 252,049 and 252,099, against 2.1234 for the hero's 4K eval of that checkpoint, logged at step 251,999. With `qk_mult` left at 1.3 (`qk16k-a0-step252k`), the drop is about 0.028. The hero's own step from 254,999 to 257,999 looks smaller (0.024) because WikiText's dip at 254,999 lowered the last 4K eval; without WikiText it is 0.032 over those 3,000 steps. So a 4K-era forecast scored against the 16K final value, as in H1 and H4 of the forecast linked above, starts about 0.03 high from the packing change alone. The offset may also drift over the remaining 16K training, so if it's cheap, one 4K eval of the final checkpoint would let these forecasts be checked at the 4K packing they were built on. How I'll compare the forecasts at the end, fixed before phase 2, is in [this addendum](https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/blob/phase2-plan-2026-10-22/addenda/2026-10-22_phase2_plan.md).

We will re-eval all checkpoints at 4k seqlen once the run is done, for those who have been tracking separate predictions. (Though a model trained at 4k->16k->65k may eval slightly differently at 4k than one that stayed at 4k the whole run, so not making any claims from our end on where that will end up).

Hash promoted multipart S3 objects when their ETag changes, and compare the result with the verified staging SHA-256 before publishing the manifest. CoreWeave produced different ETags for identical bytes, causing all 80 multipart objects in the reported transfer to fail promotion.

Write S3 staging objects with autocommit disabled and commit only after the source stream completes. A failed UploadPart now aborts the multipart upload. Small one-part uploads are verified by SHA-256 because their ETag shape changes; changed promotion ETags also require a destination read. Live CoreWeave validation has not run.

Fixes #10638

topics.title: [skyrl] Save the interference checkpoint schedule and export FP32 masters as HF
topics.head: 31efd427d838bf923047e26a9d6b6239649601f3
topics.body:
Save the interference experiment's checkpoint schedule and export its fp32 master weights as HF models.

`trainer.checkpoint_steps` lists the weight-checkpoint steps, and `trainer.optimizer_checkpoint_steps` lists the subset that keeps full optimizer state. The optimizer list must be a subset of the checkpoint list. Combining the explicit list with YAML checkpoint callbacks raises, rather than one being ignored. At the other listed steps the policy worker saves a masters-only checkpoint: the optimizer filter matches records by their `ShardedTensor.key` and keeps model records and fp32 masters while dropping moments. Masters-only saves require `optimizer_checkpoint_sharding_type: fully_reshardable`, the only format where masters and moments are separate records. A marker file records each checkpoint's optimizer state, and resuming from a masters-only checkpoint raises instead of restarting Adam with fresh moments.

`save_fp32_master_hf_model` exports a checkpoint's fp32 masters for weight analysis. Each rank loads its own master slices through the model's sharded state dict, swaps them into the live parameters for one Bridge export at `weight_dtype=float32`, and restores the weights. The export has the same HF names and layout as `save_hf_model`, with master values. A parameter without an fp32 master record raises, so a bf16-only checkpoint cannot export as fp32. Local checkpoints are read in place; S3 checkpoints stream rank tensors directly.

The GPU gate passed on a CoreWeave H100 node (`/benfeuer/wp2-fp32-export-gate-10`). It takes one Adam step on tiny Grug, saves a masters-only checkpoint, and requires three things:
- the fp32 export rounds exactly to the bf16 HF export;
- it differs from the upcast bf16 somewhere;
- its embedding equals the checkpoint's master record.

CPU tests cover schedule validation, resume guards and the masters-only filter.

Part of the Phase 0/1a work for the OPD-SFT controls experiment (CL8).

<details><summary>Original description</summary>

```markdown
The interference experiment's checkpoint schedule — fp32 master weights every
10 steps to 50 then every 25, with the full optimizer state at only three of
those steps — cannot be expressed today: checkpointing saves model and full
optimizer together at every `ckpt_interval` step, and weight analysis has no
fp32 export path.

Add `trainer.checkpoint_steps` and `trainer.optimizer_checkpoint_steps`.
Weight checkpoints follow the explicit list when one is set, otherwise the
interval. Checkpoints outside the optimizer list keep the model records and
the fp32 master params but drop the moment states through a recursive filter
over the optimizer's sharded state, and rank zero writes an
`optimizer_state.json` marker per checkpoint. Resume from latest fails with a
pointed message when that marker says masters-only, instead of silently
restarting the optimizer with fresh moments.

The fp32 export itself rides the existing checkpoint-export worker path:
`init_model_for_export` builds the export model at `trainer.bf16`, and the
DCP reader casts the fp32 master records into that dtype, so a run with
`trainer.bf16=false` exports the masters at full precision through the
bridge's own name mapping. A new GPU gate exports one tiny Grug checkpoint
both ways and requires the fp32 safetensors to round to the bf16 export byte
for byte; it runs in the GPU lane (no megatron on the CPU lane).

Schedule resolution, the callback's list mode, and the masters-only filter
are covered by CPU tests.

Part of the Phase 0/1a work for the OPD-SFT controls experiment (CL8).

```

</details>

🤖 Reworked per the review (recovered from a partial agent run and finished by hand): schedule validates optimizer-step subsets and requires fully_reshardable up front; masters filter on `leaf.key`; the callback consumes the schedule and raises on conflicts; new `export_fp32_masters` verifies fp32 master records from checkpoint metadata before reading bytes and writes sharded safetensors for WP9; resume checks the masters-only marker on both branches. topics.title: [levanter] Bound parallel model-cache shard transfers
topics.head: 80bbc990b8cc7121d0382d0203834ececb388168
topics.body:
Add bounded parallel transfers from Hugging Face to the existing Levanter shared model cache. Each worker owns one scratch directory; the distributed lock preventing concurrent writers to a snapshot remains held until every worker finishes. Transfer failure prevents the completion marker, and retries reuse completed files through the existing size checks. The default remains one worker.

Stacked on #10276, which owns resumable transfers. Reuse the revision-pinned cache identity in `resolve_cached_model_path`; leave SkyRL’s node-local HF cache unchanged.

Draft pending review of concurrency, revision enforcement, and integrity guarantees, plus a regional transfer benchmark. Retry integrity remains size-based: same-size corruption is not detected. Use resolve_cached_model_path with an immutable revision for reproducible cache identity. Regional throughput and peak local-disk usage have not been benchmarked, so no speedup is claimed.

All 18 model-cache tests pass, including parallel failure/retry and completion-marker ordering.

The broader affected suite had 504 passes, four skips, and five failures. All five reproduce on the unchanged #10276 base: four unavailable macOS-arm64 Finelog wheel cases and one temporary-checkpoint-path assertion.

topics.head: c26301534099a5db5beefbb33377243f9d155102
topics.body:
Adopt tpu-inference `1f2efcd515f4a617477bd6f7e2b8993ec2598010` and remove the Snowball reference configurations' `layer_types` overrides. The fork now includes the custom-router, weight-storage, head-padding and native layer-schedule fixes (#27–29 and #34). The vLLM pin remains `fb02daf1d7139d2adaeb0588448649591657d1e3`.

On the old a8fc5c9 pin, missing native `layer_types` means the TPU plugin config makes vLLM apply the 2048-token window to global layers. Earlier Step12 MATH500 measurements improved from 0.878/0.882 to 0.940 with the schedule override, against H100 0.944; these are historical workaround results, not validation of this new pin. See https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10270 and https://github.com/marin-community/tpu-inference/pull/34.

New-pin accelerator validation is pending. The first no-override v6e-8 job `/karan/rsi281-newpin-v6e8-r1` failed with `RuntimeError: vLLM server is not running in this environment`; the underlying startup cause still needs classification and no numerical pass is claimed. The intended gate checks all 26 actual layer windows, four KV groups, exact item-303 token identities, and teacher-forced logprobs against the eager H100 oracle. Artifacts and the reproducible validation bundle are under `gs://marin-us-east5/scratch/karan/task281/`. This draft must remain unmerged until that evidence is added.

`uv run config/update-external.py vllm --check` passes; the descriptor-generated requirement is synchronized and no lock records this source pin. The affected external-dependency and model-config tests passed (50 tests under `host-test-budget`), and the changed-file pre-commit checks passed, including Pyrefly. Reproduce with `host-test-budget uv run --no-sync pytest -q tests/inference/test_external_dependencies.py tests/evaluation/test_model_config.py`.

Refs #10270 and #10250.

topics.body:
Add `GrugModelConfig.attention_context_layout`, passed through `attention()` to the FA4 wrappers, so a run can turn off the zigzag query swap from #10170. `"zigzag"` stays the default, so 262K and every other context-parallel caller is unchanged. `"contiguous"` makes one kernel call per shard on its own query rows at offset `shard_index * local_len`, with no query split and no `ppermute`, the same code path as before #10170.

Zigzag pays off at 262K (see #10170 for the benchmarks) but slightly slows 65K, so the hero README says to keep `"zigzag"` at 262K and set `"contiguous"` at 65K, one `HERO_MODEL` line in `heuristic.py`.

The #10170 CPU position test now runs under both layouts and checks that every query row reaches the kernel at its global position. The GPU parity test for sequence-sharded queries (forward and gradients against reference attention) now also runs under both layouts. An unknown layout value raises `ValueError` at the FA4 entry point.

topics.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
topics.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. Build from this branch. The recipe below covers every model and optimizer component. Values are for d512 unless noted; the code is `experiments/grug/fast_track/{model,optimizer,heuristic,launch}.py`. **Shape** | Rung | Width D | Layers | Local (KDA) / global (MLA) layers | Heads × head dim | Batch | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | d512 | 512 | 6 | 4 / 2 | 4 × 128 | 128 | | d768 | 768 | 8 | 6 / 2 | 6 × 128 | 128 | | d1024 | 1024 | 12 | 9 / 3 | 8 × 128 | 256 | | d1280 | 1280 | 14 | 10 / 4 | 10 × 128 | 256 | - Every 4th layer and the last layer are global; all other layers are local. - The run uses a 16k vocab and sequence length 4096 with packed documents. Every ShortConv and the KDA state respect document boundaries (the KDA state resets at each document start). - Weights are initialized with std 0.5/√D. Compute is bf16. **Embedding and output** - Token embedding → RMSNorm → GatedNorm. The result is AttnRes source 0. - Output path: final AttnRes gate → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → untied lm_head (`output_proj`). - The fused lm_head + cross-entropy loop uses a vocab tile of 8192. - GatedNorm (every GatedNorm in the model) is `x · sigmoid(W_up · SiLU(W_down · x))`, with a rank-128 bottleneck. **Block (every layer)** - **Attention sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → mixer (KDA or MLA). - **MoE sublayer:** input = its AttnRes gate mix → RMSNorm → GatedNorm → MoE → ShortConv on the MoE output. - Each ShortConv is a 4-tap causal depthwise conv. **Local layers: Kimi Delta Attention** (Kimi K3's layer) - **Projections:** q/k/v are D → N·128 with full heads (no GQA). Each goes through a ShortConv followed by SiLU. q and k are L2-normalized, and q is scaled by 1/√128. - **Decay:** per-channel log-decay `g = −5·sigmoid(exp(A_log)·(x·W_a_down·W_a_up + dt_bias))`. - The gate projection has rank 128. - `A_log` is one value per head, initialized to 0. - `dt_bias` is one value per channel, initialized so the decay rate spans 0.02–0.5. - **Write strength:** `β = sigmoid(x·W_β)`, one value per head. - **Recurrence:** `S_t = (I − β·k·kᵀ)·Diag(exp(g))·S_{t−1} + β·k·vᵀ`, read out as `o_t = S_tᵀ·q_t`. - It runs as chunked Pallas kernels, with a stable block-doubling inverse inside each chunk. - **Output:** per-head RMSNorm with a learnable 128-wide scale shared across heads → full-rank per-channel gate `sigmoid(x·W_g)` → `W_o`. - No positional encoding, no window, no XSA, and no ShortConv on the branch output. **Global layers: MLA + Inkling relative position** - **q:** full-rank, D → N·128 (no Q latent). - **k and v:** k = `W_uk · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)` and v = `W_uv · RMSNorm(x·W_dkv)`. - They share one 512-wide KV latent, with a learnable RMSNorm on the latent. - Heads are 128 wide with no RoPE part. - There's no ShortConv on K, so the up-projections can be absorbed at inference. - **Scaling:** no QK-norm; `qk_mult` = 1, i.e. standard 1/√128 logit scaling. - **Position — Inkling relative-position bias**, added to the pre-softmax logits in place of RoPE: - `bias[h,i,j] = R[i,h,:] · P[:, i−j]`, where `R = x·W_r` is 16 values per head. - `P` is a bank of shape [16 × 1024] shared across heads. The relative extent is 1024. - It runs inside the FA4 attention kernel (forward, backward, and the SM90 backward pass). - **XSA** (exclusive self-attention): subtract the component of each head's output that is parallel to its own value vector. - **Output gate:** per head, `2·sigmoid(x·W_gate)`. `W_gate` is zero-initialized, so the gate is 1 at init. - The branch output also gets a ShortConv. **MoE sublayer (LatentMoE with quantile-balanced routing)** - **Experts:** 384 routed experts, top-8. Each is a SwiGLU with hidden size D/2. - **Latent space:** experts operate in a D/2-wide latent. The input goes through `W_latent_down` → RMSNorm, and the combined expert output goes back up through `W_latent_up`. - **Router:** reads the full-width token and computes logits in fp32. - Experts are selected by top-(8+1) on bias-adjusted logits, where the 9th logit is the threshold α. - Combine weights are the sigmoid of the unbiased logits, renormalized to sum to 2.5. - **Quantile balancing:** each step, each expert's threshold β is the global (1 − K/E) quantile of the logit margins (logit − α), read from a 10k-bin histogram. The router bias is set to −β. - The router bias is not trained by gradient. - **Capacity:** capacity factor 1.15, with pooled-wave expert-parallel dispatch. Receiver ranks are sort-based and the expand backward is gather-based. - **Shared experts:** 2 shared SwiGLU experts that bypass the latent: D → D/2 hidden → D. - **Fused projections:** - The router, latent-down, and both shared experts' gate/up projections run as one GEMM. - The shared experts' down-projections run as one GEMM. **Residual stream: Block Attention Residuals** - **Sources:** the embedding source, one running sum per completed block of sublayer outputs, and the running partial sum of the current block. - The model has 8 blocks. Block sums use the raw sublayer outputs. - **Gates:** every sublayer (attention and MoE) has its own gate, and there is one final gate before the output norm. Each gate has one learned pseudo-query `q ∈ ℝᴰ`, zero-initialized so every gate starts as a uniform average. - **Mixing:** per token, `logitᵢ = q · rms_norm(sourceᵢ)`, using a parameter-free (frozen) RMS key norm, then `softmax` over sources and a weighted sum of the raw sources. - **Implementation:** - Each completed block is scored once against every gate that reads it. - Backward: at d512 the layer's forward intermediates are saved. At d768–d1280 each layer is recomputed. At d1280 the attention branch is also rematerialized. - The model keeps one layer stack per mixer kind. **Optimizer** | Group | Update rule | LR | Parameters | |---|---|---|---| | `muonh` | MuonH | MuonH LR | all attention and MoE matrices: MLA `W_q`/`W_dkv`/`W_uk`/`W_uv`/`W_o`; KDA `W_q`/`W_k`/`W_v`/`W_o`/`W_g`; experts; shared experts; latent down/up. Also every GatedNorm `W_down`/`W_up`. | | `kda_beta` | MuonH | 2 × MuonH LR | KDA `W_β` | | `adamh` | AdamH | MuonH LR | lm_head (`output_proj`) | | `adam` | Adam | Adam LR | token embedding; router; attention output gate; router bias slot (overwritten by QB); all 1-D norm gains; ShortConv kernels; KDA `W_a_down`/`W_a_up`, `A_log`, `dt_bias`; Inkling `W_r` and `P` | | `attn_res_query` | Adam | 0.1 × Adam LR | the AttnRes pseudo-queries | - **MuonH:** Nesterov momentum 0.95 → Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (5 quintic steps, bucketed across same-shape matrices) → a step along that direction, then projection back onto the matrix's Frobenius sphere. Each matrix's norm stays fixed at its init value. - **AdamH:** the Adam direction with the same Frobenius-sphere (hyperball) projection. - **Adam:** β1 0.9. Only the router and the attention output gate get decoupled weight decay (0.02). No other parameter gets weight decay, and there's no gradient clipping. - **Schedule:** 1% warmup, then linear decay to 0.05× peak. - **Peak values** from `MoeHeuristic` (they depend on tokens, width and batch): - Adam LR = `0.0876 · tokens^−0.346 · D^−0.345 · √(tokens per batch)`. - MuonH LR = 13/3 × Adam LR. - β2 = `0.999^(tokens per batch / 131072)`. - ε = `9.68e−18 · √(steps)`. - At d512 with 2384 steps: MuonH LR 0.0227, Adam LR 0.0052, β2 0.996, ε 4.7e−16. comments.body:
Some ideas to get started. Treat this as a general pool of ideas, that indicates the spirit of what can be tried.
1. https://blog.tilderesearch.com/blog/online-kl-shampoo. Consider interactions with hyperball and selectively replace matrices.
2. Add a second embedding table with its own random init. Attn residuals queries both embedding tables, treating them as unique inputs.
3. Lets add value embeddings. That is, a second embedding table that gets added to V on the MLA layers. So take KV latent-> project to num_heads of size 128. Then do values = lambda1*values + lambda2*value_embeds[layer_i]. lambda 1 init to 1, lambda2 init to 0. value_embeds has [vocab_size, num_heads*head_dim, num_mla_layers] dimension. Can also try gated value embeds, where instead of lambda2, its conditional on residual stream via sigmoid(linear(x)).
4. Add learnable scalars to each submodule output, that feeds into attention residuals. May be worth tracking and plotting these in wandb, to see if indicates any architecture changes will help.
5. Try different variations of linear attention to replace KDA.
6. It has been shown in many places that the final couple layers of attention dont prefer to attend to outputs from the final MLPs. See if there is any change to attention residuals to help make this more natural.
7. Adding an lm_head auxillary loss to the output of layer 1 for the first X (say 500) steps can help give the routed experts a cleaner role early. Unclear how this interacts with attention residuals.
8. Hash routing on first layer.
9. Instead of Adam/AdamH on embed and lm_head, look into other optimizers here that have shown promise in literature.
10. Do any weights benefit from extremely different beta1/beta2/momentum terms, or swapping their optimizer group.
11. Update the router behavior (sigmoid vs softmax), normalizing over picked experts vs not, sampling over experts instead of top k).
12. Null routing (enable tokens to select null experts which skips their computation, dynamic compute per token).
13. Multi-token-prediction.
14. Sparse attention.

If users give comments with singular specific ideas, give it priority over this laundry list.

🤖 **Agent check-in.**

**Identity:** Claude Code (model `claude-opus-5-5`, 1M context), running locally on @ClassicLarry's machine in the `marin` repo.

**Prior context:** a fresh session with no conversation history. I carry the persistent auto-memory notes from earlier sessions in this repo (Iris/CoreWeave job submission quirks, W&B 128-char run-name limit, GB200 gang-retry flakes, grug MoE perf notes). I have no prior runs on this issue. I will build from `fasttrack-moe-kma` @ `4eba59cafa` as the issue specifies.

**Prompt I was given (verbatim):**

> Your job is to execute on https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451. Continue working until told to stop. First post a comment showing this exact prompt. Indicate your identity and prior context. Stay alert for human input via the github issue.

**Next:** read `experiments/grug/fast_track/{README.md,agent.md}` and the code, measure baseline throughput on cw-us-east-02a, then launch batch 1 (5–10 d512 runs drawn from the idea list above). I will post one comment per batch and edit it as runs finish.

🤖 **Batch 1: cheap architecture adds from the idea list, an LR check, and a noise and profile baseline** (d512, 2475 steps) — **done**

**Goal.** Test the lowest-cost ideas from @ClassicLarry's list: `#2` (second embedding table), `#3` (value embeddings, both forms), and `#4` (learnable sublayer output scalars, logged to W&B). Also check whether the `MoeHeuristic` LR, which was fit on the old baseline architecture, is still right for KMA (×1.5 and ×0.67 on both LRs). Add a seed-1 baseline to calibrate noise, and a 60-step profile to find speed levers. Speed counts as a win under the fixed-time objective.

**Assumption (I'll correct it next batch if it's wrong).** None of these changes adds meaningful compute, so all runs use the baseline's 2475 steps instead of a separate probe. After each run I check its steady-state ex/s. If it is more than about 1% below 660, I rerun at `round(480 × ex/s / 128)` steps. Branch [`ladderclimb_v1_batch01`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/eb26f3cbc9) @ `eb26f3cbc9`: every change is gated by a `--model-set` / `--opt-set` flag and defaults to off.

**Implementation details**
- **ve:** each MLA layer gets a [16384 × N·128] table, and `v = λ1·v + λ2·VE[token]` (λ1 = 1, λ2 = 0 at init). The tables, λ and the gate go to Adam at the Adam LR, like `token_embed`.
- **veg:** `v = λ1·v + sigmoid(x·W)·VE[token]`, with one gate per head. `W` is zero-initialized, so the gate starts at 0.5.
- **osc:** a scalar initialized to 1 on each attention and MoE sublayer output before it enters the AttnRes history (Adam). Logged as `train/attn_res/scale_{attn,mlp}_L*`.

The routed-expert output magnitude is capped by MuonH's sphere and the 2.5 combine renorm, and it wants to grow.
- **Profile (8×H100, d512, ~187 ms/step).** Compute is ~155 ms: elementwise fusions ~61, GEMMs ~43, sort/scatter/gather ~23, KDA ~14, FA4 ~7. Exposed EP all-to-all is ~18 ms, and the host gap between steps is ~6 ms.

Under the bf16 compute policy, the gather's transpose scatter-adds every token's cotangent directly into a **bf16** table. That means contended bf16 atomics, with frequent tokens' gradients rounded at every add. A single-GPU microbenchmark puts the fp32 scatter at 0.2 ms. The same scatter is why ve, veg and emb2 were slow: each extra table adds one.

🤖 **Batch 9: looped models (@neel04's request): tied looping, with and without growth, with input injection** (d512, paired seed 0 vs qk_mult-2.5 base **3.0858**)

**Addresses** @neel04's comment. It follows [slowrun#92](https://github.com/qlabs-eng/slowrun/pull/92) (1× for 70% of training, then 2×) and [arXiv 2609.19107](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19107) (boundary operator `Norm(h) + α·e`, growth partway through training, backprop through all passes, and FLOPs of every pass counted). Branch [`ladderclimb_v1_batch09`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c2803601b0).

**How it maps onto KMA** (`loop_passes`, `loop_grow_step`):
- **The looped core is the whole 6-layer stack**, weights tied. Each pass extends the Block AttnRes history. Pass 2's gates read the embedding, every pass-1 block, and the pass-2 blocks so far. Pass 2 has its own zero-initialized AttnRes pseudo-queries, so its gates start as uniform averages over that longer history.
- **Input injection.** At the start of each extra pass, the running partial is initialized to `α·e`, where e is the normalized embedding source and α is learned (init 1, Adam), and the pass's layers write onto it. The AttnRes gates already see e as source 0. This is the explicit re-injection from both references. The AttnRes softmax already normalizes what each sublayer reads, which plays the part of `Norm(h)`.
- **Growth** uses a step-gated `lax.cond`. Before the growth step only pass 1 executes, at full base speed. After it both passes run, with gradients through both. The router biases are shared per physical layer; their QB statistics are averaged over the passes.
- **Fixed-time steps.** Two passes run at 0.506× the base throughput (80-step probe: 381.8 vs 754.1 ex/s), so every run is given 8 minutes of train-step time:
  - loop2 throughout: 1426 steps.
  - Grow at 70%: N solves `0.7N/751 + 0.3N/380 = 480/128`, so N = 2179 and growth is at step 1525.
  - Grow at 50%: N = 1892, growth at step 946.
- **Not in this batch: untied growth**, where the core is copied at the growth step and the copies train separately. It changes the parameter tree and optimizer state mid-run, so it needs trainer work. It's next if tied growth looks promising.

What the average distribution shows (final step):
- **Attention gates mostly read the immediately preceding layer's output**, a learned residual stream. The weight on it decays with depth: L1 0.73, L2 0.66, L3 0.48, L4 0.43.
- **The last MLA layer (L5) is the exception.** It puts 0.32 on L2's output, more than on L3 (0.17) or L4 (0.15), so it skips back over the two most recent layers. That fits idea `#6` (late attention layers don't want the latest sublayer outputs).
- **MoE gates mostly read their own layer's attention output (the partial):** 0.85 at L0, down to 0.40 at L4. L5's MoE instead splits across L3 out (0.18), L4 out (0.31) and the partial (0.31).
- **The final gate feeding the lm_head uses almost only the last three layers:** L3 0.16, L4 0.33, L5 0.41. The embedding and L0–L2 get ≤ 0.05 there, although every attention gate keeps 0.13–0.27 on the embedding.
- **The pattern forms early.** By step 1408 it is nearly final, and at step 100 the gates are still close to uniform.

- **A smaller MLA KV latent clearly hurts:** 512 → 256 gives +0.016 and → 128 gives +0.019, with no measurable speedup at d512. Attention there is a small share of step time. Batch 15 tests cross-layer reuse instead: the last MLA layer reads the first MLA layer's KV latent, which halves the MLA cache.

L4 KDA pays almost zero attention to all prior attention layers. That is suspicious. Perhaps the state tracking nature of KDA gets overwhelmed with too much cross token smearing. Block attention residuals doesn't let KDA layers pick out just the prior MLPs.

Lets try full attention residuals, but block L4 KDA from attending to any prior attention layer outputs. If that improves over the full attention residuals baseline, it indicates an opportunity. We should also assess the impact of dropping sconv from the attention outputs and mlp outputs.

Standard attention residuals follows a 'push' methodology. Each layer output gets to decide what future layers it gets propogated to, since the queries are static per layer. Alternatively, one could use a 'pull' methodology. Every output submodule has a static key, and the query is defined by the current residual stream activation. Lets try that approach, zeroing the keys at init. Also try a hybrid, where we follow standard attn residuals, but just vary the embed. It seems odd that the embed should pre-decide how much it appears in each subsequent layer. To get the embed logit, run a linear projection over the current residual stream. (So we can think of that as the query is the residual stream, and the key is a learned weight).

🤖 **Batch 18: AttnRes routing structure (@ClassicLarry's latest comment), ShortConv ablations, and a linear-attention variant** (d512, 2817 steps, paired seed 0 on the current bundle with z-loss kept: qk 2.5 + β1 0.8 + no GatedNorms = **3.0854**)

**Addresses** the comment about L4 KDA ignoring earlier attention outputs, the ShortConv ablations, and "pull" vs "push" AttnRes. Branch [`ladderclimb_v1_batch14` @ `5eb01900ba`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/5eb01900ba).

1. **Full AttnRes with L4's KDA attention gate blocked from every earlier attention output** (`attn_res_mask_attn_for=4`). That gate reads only the embedding and the MoE outputs; the masked sources get a −1e9 logit. It is compared against full AttnRes on the same base (`lc1-b18-full`). The batch-15 full run used z-loss 0, so it's rerun here. If the masked version wins, it points to KDA wanting to pick out MoE outputs, which Block AttnRes can't do.
2. **ShortConv ablations:** drop the conv on the attention sublayer output (`sconv_sites=mlp`; only the MLA layers had one, since KDA's output never did), on the MoE output (`sconv_sites=attn`), and both (`sconv_sites=`). KDA's own q/k/v convs stay.
3. **Pull AttnRes** (`attn_res_pull`). Each source has a static learned key k_n, zero-initialized (the running partial has its own). A gate's query is its **current residual stream**: the RMS-normed plain sum of the sources it can see. So logit_n = rms_norm(Σ sources) · k_n. Keys train with Adam at 0.1×, like the push queries. At init it's identical to push (uniform mix).
4. **Hybrid:** push AttnRes, except the **embedding's logit is pulled**: a learned zero-initialized vector per gate, dotted with the gate's RMS-normed current stream (`attn_res_pull_embed`). The embedding no longer pre-decides its weight in each layer.
5. **Gated-DeltaNet-style per-head decay in KDA** (`kda_decay_per_head`): one log-decay per head instead of per channel. This is idea `#5`, a different linear attention.

A depth-1 **MTP** head (idea `#13`: predict t+2 from h_t + W·norm(embed(t+1)) through the shared lm_head, weight 0.3) is implemented at [`06bbf60466`](/06bbf60466). It adds a second lm_head pass, which is expensive at d512, The probe measured 689.6 vs 754.1 ex/s (−8.6%), so it runs at 2576 fixed-time steps.

🤖 **Batch 19: a real go at Online KL-Shampoo, applied selectively (@ClassicLarry), and the ShortConv comparison at d768**

**Addresses** the comment asking to give [Online KL-Shampoo](https://blog.tilderesearch.com/blog/online-kl-shampoo) a real go, applied selectively so we can see its direction per matrix family, and to compare dropping all branch-output ShortConvs at d768.

**What the earlier attempt found** (branch `okls-optimizer`, on the pre-KMA baseline). It replaced MuonH on *every* matrix with OKLS's own muP-scaled, AdamC-decayed update. It never beat MuonH (+0.005 to +0.027 over an LR sweep, 16% slower), and its one hyperball variant crashed before step 25. The crash matches the broken-scipy job environment seen elsewhere, so it was never actually tested.

**This version** ([`7d5f5dd116`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/7d5f5dd116)):
- `okls_targets` picks matrix families; everything else stays on MuonH. The families are:
  - **attn**: MLA `w_q/w_o/w_dkv/w_uk/w_uv` and KDA `w_q/w_k/w_v/w_o/w_g`
  - **routed**: the expert gate/up/down stacks
  - **shared**: the shared experts
  - **latent**: the LatentMoE down/up projections
  - **gated_norm**: the GatedNorms
- For the selected matrices, the **direction** is the OKLS whitening `U = S_a^{-1/2} · N · S_b^{-1/2}`. Here N is Nesterov momentum, S_a/S_b are the Kronecker-factor EMAs with the blog's β1 0.9684 / β2 0.9482, and the roots come from 10-step Scaled-CANS coupled Newton-Schulz. **That direction then takes MuonH's hyperball step at the MuonH LR.** Only the direction changes, so there's no new LR scale to tune, and the matrices stay on their Frobenius spheres like the rest of the model.
- CPU checks: the 6 ported OKLS math tests pass (CANS inverse-sqrt accuracy, warm start, whitening conditioning, norm-preserving hyperball step). Routing is verified per family.
- 80-step throughput probes are running for 4 selections. OKLS roots cost O(d³) per matrix, so each gets its own fixed-time step count. Then the full runs go, paired against the current bundle's seed 0 (3.0854):
  - attention only (fp32 CANS)
  - routed experts only (fp16 CANS, since there are 384 small matrices per layer)
  - shared + latent (fp32)
  - all families (fp16)
  - Promising families get LR and β2 variations after that.

**On KDA at layer 0 and a decay that "looks at the state first".** The observation is right, and it holds for every KDA layer, not just layer 0. KDA's forget gate (like GDN's and Mamba's) is **input-dependent but not state-dependent**: g_t = f(x_t), where at layer 0 x_t is just the normed embedding.
- **Why it's built that way:** the chunked algorithm needs every position's gates *before* running the recurrence, which is what makes it parallel. A decay that reads S_{t−1} makes the layer a nonlinear RNN (LSTM/sLSTM-style), which can only run step by step. That's the trade Kimi, GDN and Mamba all make.
- **What already reads the state:** the delta rule itself. S_t = (I − β kkᵀ) Diag(e^g) S_{t−1} + β k vᵀ first erases whatever S currently stores along key k (β k (kᵀS)), and only then writes v. So "how much to overwrite" is content-addressed against the state; the per-channel decay is only the context-free background forgetting.
- **Two cheap probes of the intuition that stay parallel:**
  1. `kda_decay_conv`: a 4-tap causal ShortConv over the rank-128 decay input, so g_t sees the last few tokens instead of just its own (the q/k/v paths already have such convs). It applies to all KDA layers.

🤖 **Batch 22: which KDA layers need decay and write strength, and "push" decay (@ClassicLarry)** (d512, token-matched at 2817 steps, paired seed 0 vs the gate-2 recipe `lc1-b17-bzl` = **3.0834**)

**Addresses** the comment asking to drop KDA's decay (α) and β one layer at a time, and to set up a "push" decay where each written token chooses its own half-life.

**1. Per-layer ablations** ([`d80ac50049`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/d80ac50049)). `kda_no_decay_layers=L` sets g = 0 in layer L, so that state never forgets. `kda_no_beta_layers=L` sets β = 1, a full-strength delta-rule write. The KDA layers are 0, 1, 2 and 4 (3 and 5 are MLA). A CPU check confirms only the targeted layer's parameters stop receiving gradient.

**2. Push decay: the math** ([`d80ac50049`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/d80ac50049)).
- **Pull (current KDA):** `S_t = (I − β_t k_t k_tᵀ) Diag(e^{g_t}) S_{t−1} + β_t k_t v_tᵀ`. The **reader** t sets one decay applied to everything already stored.
- **Push (ideal):** write i sets its own rate λ_i, and its contribution at time t is `e^{−λ_i (t−i)} · β_i k_i v_iᵀ`. Arbitrary per-write rates don't compose into one running state.
- **Push with buckets:** keep M delta-rule states, each decaying at its own **static, learned, per-channel** rate λ_m that no token controls. The writer splits its write with weights π_{t,m}:
  `S⁽ᵐ⁾_t = (I − β_t π_{t,m} k kᵀ) Diag(e^{−λ_m}) S⁽ᵐ⁾_{t−1} + β_t π_{t,m} k_t v_tᵀ`, and the read is `o_t = Σ_m S⁽ᵐ⁾_tᵀ q_t`.
  - With M = 2 this is your "second S": a slow state and a fast one, where each token decides what fraction of itself is temporary. The "subtract the decayed copy from the main S" form is the same thing written differently: S_perm + S_temp.
  - Each bucket is an ordinary KDA recurrence with a constant g and a scaled β, so the existing chunked kernel runs it unchanged. The cost is one extra kernel pass per bucket, about 8% step time per bucket at d512. These runs are token-matched, to check for a loss effect first.
  - **Parameters:** `push_decay` [M, heads, 128] holds the bucket decay logits, initialized log-spaced over a |g| range. `W_push` [D, heads·M] is zero-initialized, so the split starts uniform. Both train with Adam like the other KDA decay parameters.
- **Hybrid:** each bucket decays at the reader's g plus its own static rate, clamped to KDA's −5 per-token floor. Both writer and reader get a say.

**Addresses** four comments: AttnRes on the shared vs routed experts; low-rank router variants; combining [Residual Matrix Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22696) with AttnRes; and a shift toward MFU gains if these don't pan out.

**1. Which part of the MoE input needs AttnRes** ([`c786c05f69`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c786c05f69)). Batch 21 found that the MoE input reading the straight sum costs +0.028. This splits it: the shared experts only, the routed path only (router + latent-down), and the router alone. The router run separates the routing decision from the expert input. The runs are full AttnRes at 2712 steps, paired against 3.0774.

**2. Low-rank router** ([`c786c05f69`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/c786c05f69)): `logits = f(x W_r↓) W_r↑` at rank 32 or 128, where f is identity, a learnable RMSNorm, or SiLU. W_r↓ replaces the router column block in the fused MoE-input GEMM. The logits are computed in fp32 as before, both matrices train with Adam and the router weight decay, and QB balancing is unchanged. Token-matched, paired against the gate-2 recipe (3.0834).

**3. RMT × AttnRes** ([`82abc339ac`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/82abc339ac)). RMT stores sublayer outputs in an outer-product matrix and reads it with **R per-head read keys**. AttnRes is already a residual *memory* with one slot per source, read by a softmax over pseudo-query scores; the dissection found that different readers (V and MoE vs Q/K) want different mixes. Two variants borrow RMT's per-head, per-reader retrieval:
- **Multi-head AttnRes** (`attn_res_heads=H`): each gate's pseudo-query is split into H chunks of D/H. Chunk h scores the sources on its own channel slice, with the same parameter-free RMS key norm, and mixes that slice with its own softmax. It's H retrieval heads over the same memory, adds no parameters, and reduces exactly to today's AttnRes at H = 1. H = 4 and 8.
- **A separate V-input gate** (`attn_res_v_gate`): each layer gets a second zero-init pseudo-query for its value projections, so V reads its own mix while Q/K keep the attention gate's.
- Heavier RMT pieces (a matrix residual with outer-product writes) would replace AttnRes rather than combine with it. I'm holding those unless these show signal.

**4. MFU.** A fresh 60-step profile of the gate-2 recipe is first in the queue, to pick the low-hanging items. One suspect is already visible: the per-step logging I added (about 70 AttnRes weight, query-norm and qk_mult scalars every step) goes through the blocking host loop. Recent runs sit at ~740 ex/s vs ~751 before it. Making the logging sparse is the first cheap item, and the profile will rank the rest.

🤖 **Batch 25: two-query AttnRes, blended AttnRes, and spreading the MoE input** (branch `ladderclimb_v1_batch14`, d512, paired against the current best, 3.0834)

These follow up [the two-query / λ-blend comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5844691943) and [the MLP input-spread comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5844712356). Every flag defaults off. The changes apply to every AttnRes gate, including the final one.

**Two queries per gate (`attn_res_dual_query`).** Each gate keeps its zero-init query `q_a` and adds a second query `q_b ~ N(0, σ)`, so both start close to an even mix over the sources.
- Each query takes its own softmax-weighted sample of the sources, giving `mix_a` and `mix_b`.
- Merge per token: `s = σ(rms_norm(stream) · w + b)`, input = `s · mix_a + (1 − s) · mix_b`. Here `stream` is the plain sum of the gate's sources.
- `w` and `b` are zero-init, so `s = ½` at init.
- σ is tried at 0.005 and 0.02. The initial logit spread is about σ·√D, i.e. 0.11 and 0.45.

**Blend with the standard residual (`attn_res_blend`).** Input = `λ₁ · attnres_mix + λ₂ · mean(sources)`, with learned scalars per gate, both init 1.
- I used the mean rather than the sum. The RMSNorm that follows makes the two equivalent, apart from how λ₂ is parameterized.
- **static:** λ are plain scalars.
- **dynamic:** λₖ also gets `+ rms_norm(stream) · wₖ`, a zero-init per-token term.
- Caveat: at init the AttnRes mix *is* the uniform mean, and the following RMSNorm cancels scale. So the λ gradient is about 0 until the gate moves off uniform. The params are on Adam, which rescales small gradients, so they will still move.

**MLP input spread.** Here is how I read the idea. How well a neuron can choose which fraction of tokens it fires on depends on the spread of `w·x`. If `x` sits on a small, anisotropic manifold (a large shared mean direction and a few dominant directions), most `w` see little variance, and the high-variance directions dominate learning.
- **Whitening** the input (`x → C^{-1/2}(x − μ)`) makes every direction carry unit variance, so any `w` sees the same spread.
- For a linear layer that follows, whitening is a reparameterization of `W`, so it adds no expressivity. It changes what Adam and Muon do: it is K-FAC's / Shampoo's input-side factor applied to the activations. Muon orthogonalizes the update but ignores the input covariance, so that factor is what our optimizer is missing.
- It also changes the router, since QB reads the whitened input.
- The matching knobs:
  - **center:** subtract the batch mean (over all tokens, stop-gradient) from every MoE input.
  - **whiten, p:** `x → (x − μ) · C^{−p/2}`, with `C` the batch covariance. Its eigenvalues are trace-normalized, then shrunk by `+1e-3`, via `eigh` on a 512×512 matrix. Stop-gradient, so there is no backward through `eigh`. p = 0.5 is half-whitening (Shampoo's exponent); p = 1 is full ZCA whitening.
- Caveats:
  - Batch statistics leak about 1/N of each token into all others (N ≈ 130k tokens), and eval uses the eval batch's own statistics. If whitening wins, I'll switch to EMA statistics from previous steps, which are strictly causal.
  - These runs are **data-matched** (2817 steps). If one wins, I'll check its throughput and fixed-time step count.

Other ideas for the spread question (not yet run): a spread penalty on the MoE input's covariance (for example log-det or effective rank), an EMA-whitened version as above, or whitening only the expert down path while leaving the router alone.
